Content: This shift from optimizing for keywords to optimizing for the moment behind the search is probably one of the most important mindset changes for marketers right now. Too many small businesses still think visibility is the goal, when the real goal is solving a customer&39;s problem in the exact context they are experiencing it. If AI can understand intent better than ever, are we creating content that genuinely answers real business questions or are we still writing for yesterday&39;s algorithm? How many companies are losing qualified opportunities because their content attracts clicks but never builds trust or moves people toward a decision? And if AI increasingly values complete, structured answers, shouldn&39;t businesses also rethink how they measure content success beyond rankings alone?The same principle applies across marketing. More traffic does not automatically create more revenue. Faster response times, stronger follow up, clearer positioning, and consistent conversion often have a bigger impact than another blog post or another SEO tactic. Businesses that understand customer moments instead of chasing marketing activity will build more predictable growth because they are solving real problems, not simply competing for attention.

Content: day-3(this is aigenerated ,i am not claming i wrote this)Summary of Today&39;s Lecture – My Understanding What is Amazon EC2? Amazon EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) is a core AWS service that provides scalable virtual servers, known as instances, in the cloud. Instead of buying physical hardware, you can rent a virtual machine that comes with a combination of CPU, RAM, storage, and networking capabilities, all configured to your specific needs. Why do we need EC2? Managing EC2 instances is much easier and more cost-effective compared to maintaining on-premises physical servers. With EC2, you follow a pay-as-you-go model, meaning you only pay for what you use. This eliminates the massive upfront costs and maintenance headaches associated with physical infrastructure, similar to the cloud advantages discussed in earlier lectures. Key Concepts Covered: EC2 Instance Types: AWS offers a wide range of instance types optimized for different workloads: General Purpose (e.g., t2.micro, t3, m5): A balance of compute, memory, and networking. Ideal for web servers, small databases, and development environments. Compute Optimized (e.g., c5, c6g): Designed for high-performance compute tasks like batch processing and high-traffic web servers. Memory Optimized (e.g., r5, x1e): Optimized for memory-intensive workloads like in-memory databases and real-time analytics. Storage Optimized (e.g., i3, d3): Designed for high-speed, low-latency access to local storage. Regions & Availability Zones: EC2 instances can be launched in different geographic regions and availability zones around the world, allowing you to deploy applications closer to your users for better performance and high availability. Security Groups: These act as virtual firewalls for your EC2 instances, controlling inbound and outbound traffic. You define rules to allow specific traffic, like SSH (port 22) or HTTP (port 8080). Key Pairs: Key pairs are used for secure SSH access to your EC2 instances. You download a private key file (.pem) and use it to connect to your instance. Hands-on Project: Deploying Jenkins on AWS The practical part of the session involved a step-by-step project to deploy Jenkins (a popular automation server) on an EC2 instance. The key steps were: Launch an EC2 Instance: Create an EC2 instance using the AWS Free Tier. This typically involves choosing an Amazon Linux 2 or Ubuntu AMI and a t2.micro instance type. Configure Security: Set up a key pair for secure SSH access and configure the security group to allow traffic on port 8080 (the default port for Jenkins). Connect via SSH: Use the SSH command with your key pair to connect to the instance. Install Jenkins: Once connected, update the system, install Java (a prerequisite for Jenkins), add the Jenkins repository, and install Jenkins. Access Jenkins: After installation, access the Jenkins web interface by entering the instance&39;s public IP address followed by port 8080 in a web browser. (For a clearer understanding and hands-on demonstrations, please watch the full video.) Thank you, Abhishek Veeramalla anna, for your clear explanation and practical approach to learning EC2 and deploying real-world applications.

Content: If you are facing the following error while starting Jenkins:jenkins.service: Start request repeated too quickly.jenkins.service: Failed with result &39;exit-code&39;.Failed to start jenkins.service - Jenkins Continuous Integration Server.Make sure that the correct JAVA_HOME path is set in the Jenkins configuration file.Edit the file:sudo nano /etc/default/jenkinsAdd or update this line (based on your installed Java version):JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-21-openjdk-amd64Save the file, then restart Jenkins:sudo systemctl daemon-reloadsudo systemctl restart jenkinssudo systemctl status jenkinsThis should resolve the issue if it is related to an incorrect or missing Java configuration.

Content: Here are the key sections covered in this bootcamp session: Introduction to Databricks: The host explains the shift from traditional single-machine processing to modern cloud-based data platforms (30:32 - 51:07). Databricks in Real-World Workflows: Discussion on how companies use the platform, including data architecture, the importance of the gold layer, and the role of various users like data analysts and scientists (52:11 - 58:08). SQL Warehouse & Compute: An explanation of serverless SQL warehouses, including how to scale them for presentations and cost management (1:25:01 - 1:29:49). Working with Data: Practical demonstrations on how to upload data, the difference between volumes vs. delta tables, and querying data using the SQL editor (1:30:49 - 1:46:06). Catalog & Metadata: A deep dive into the Unity Catalog and the importance of metadata for AI applications and data lineage (2:46:44 - 2:52:47). Data Analytics & Visualization: How to perform Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) within Databricks, creating queries, and building simple dashboards (2:54:05 - 3:14:29). Generative AI (Genie): A demonstration of Genie (BI AI), which allows users to interact with data using natural language prompts (3:22:44 - 3:28:03). blessings and thanks Barra

Content: LmaoI did a travel chatbot pretty much like this. 2 years ago. Each agent had a prompt and produced a .md file that had been sent to the next one, precisely because debugging it was hell*1. First guardrails - filter irrelevant and politically incorrect queries. We do not want our bot to even engage in queries like "I&39;d like to go to a place without Black people", or the chatbot helping kids do their homework.2. Sorting - is this the first entry, what do we know already, what are we missing, is the user done with requirements.3. Extract user requirements.4. Match vs embeddings + generate synonyms (i.e. we had skiing trips where the word "snow" did not happen once, it was "hit the slopes" for example, so both embedding and argument extraction had to synonymize).5. See how many arguments we have - if we know when, where, for whom, what&39;s the activity etc. (so we know everything), we return trips. That&39;s rarely the case, so we categorize requirements we got from the input, to ask for the missing ones.6. Response - reiterate collected requirements + matching deal/hardcoded "no" (for politically incorrect/irrelevant - hardcoded because we really do not want the bot to answer "Armenian genocide is a complex issue", we had a safe and neutral answer that could not be published on twitter)/ a question for more requirements/"we have no matches, do you wish to see partial matches?".It worked until the client started tinkering with the prompts. But the idea was that each stage had to publish a concise input for a subsequent stage, limiting the context. Nothing was actually receiveing the entire conversation, only a so-far summary of it appended as needed. Signal2noise ratio is a bitch.* debugging story: because the agent&39;s tone statement was "to inspire people to travel", it was making up trips that weren&39;t available, i.e. "I want to go somewhere warm this spring" -> "how about crossing Sahara desert on a camel&39;s back under a sea of stars?" -> "sounds good" -> "sorry, we got nothing like it"

Content: I absolutely fixed it, find me Built a trusted gate that sits between an AI coding agent&39;s proposed shell/file actions and what actually runs — it sorts every action by whether it&39;s reversible, auto-runs the safe stuff (reads, tests), and pauses or blocks the irreversible (rm -rf, force-push, network egress, anything reaching outside the project). The core allow/deny logic is machine-checked with Z3 — proven for every possible input, not just tested — and I threw ~2,000,000 adversarial commands at it with zero auto-allowed bypasses. Honest caveat though: it&39;s a policy layer you run over a real OS sandbox, and it governs what the agent can reach, not whether its code is any good.

Content: Fun fact regarding the lack of encryption on X10/IBM Home Director back in 1996: At the time, strong cryptography was legally classified by the US government as an export-controlled munition under ITAR (International Traffic in Arms Regulations)—right alongside tanks and fighter jets.Because of this, tech companies weren&39;t legally allowed to export software with encryption stronger than 40 bits without a weapon-export license. Implementing advanced encryption would have forced IBM to build two completely separate domestic and international versions of the software, so a lot of consumer companies just left it unencrypted to avoid the legal nightmare. The rules didn&39;t finally change until early 2000!

Content: Thank you. I found this interesting and I do feel a need to respond at some depth.Powerful Broken People Meaning Trauma AI and UK Reasonable Adjustments David Kossoff my father and the search for meaning “But he knoweth the way that I take when he hath tried me I shall come forth as gold”(Job 23.10) “And after the fire a still small voice” (1 Kings 19.12) “When he was yet a great way off his father saw him and had compassion” (Luke 15.20) Here is an example of how Viktor Frankl and his championing of meaning sometimes enters my life unexpectedly and welcomingly as a friend I yet never met. I am sharing this reflection on my fathers life and the meaning he found through David Kossoff who visited the care home where my father spent his final days. Kossoffs gentle presence and the way he read biblical stories without judgement gave my father an enduring sense of peace that had evaded him all his life. Kossoff read these stories with compassion rather than condemnation offering wounded people the feeling of being accepted rather than blamed. I believe he was moved to this work partly by the convictions of his faith and partly by the grief of losing his own son Paul Kossoff of the band Free whose life was cut short by drugs taken in an attempt to numb the pain of his new family the band fracturing around him. My fathers life began with loss. Orphaned at four he entered the world already carrying a wound that shaped everything that followed. He was almost the same age as David Kossoff and perhaps that closeness of generation made Kossoffs voice feel less like a distant storyteller and more like someone who understood the world he had lived through. As a young man he became a Welsh Guard driving a Churchill tank during the D Day advance a place where nations were in conflict yet individuals on all sides were simply caught in historys machinery. He slept on the Normandy beach witnessed death at close range and lost a friend he had bonded with in the intensity of war. The trauma of those experiences never left him. After the war he fell into depression attempted suicide and struggled with memories he could not escape. Later psychiatric mismanagement and prescription drug interference contributed to an assault on my mother leading to a prison sentence that was cut short only when they realised he was ill. He died at sixty one of lung cancer my mother at seventy two of the same disease. In the final period of his life he lived in a rest home for people who were psychologically distressed in St Albans. He told me that David Kossoff had been there. Kossoff was known for visiting places where people suffered offering not doctrine but gentleness. His retellings of biblical stories Job Elijah in the cave the Prodigal Son were shaped not by theology but by compassion. He spoke to the wounded the frightened the ashamed the abandoned. For someone like my father who had lived through war loss guilt institutionalisation and illness Kossoffs stories could have offered a rare moment of recognition suffering without blame brokenness without condemnation and the possibility of peace without triumph. Viktor Frankl wrote that meaning can be found even in unavoidable suffering not by erasing pain but by placing it within a human story. Kossoffs voice may have helped my father do exactly that. A man who had been orphaned traumatised punished and misunderstood might have felt for a moment that his life was not meaningless that his suffering belonged to the long human struggle for dignity and understanding. I honour my fathers experience in my own creative work by carrying forward the spirit of what comforted him compassion for damaged people gentleness toward suffering and the belief that even the most wounded lives contain meaning. His story reminds me that peace often arrives quietly like Elijahs still small voice and that brokenness does not erase worth. Jonathan Pageau ARC 2026 summary Jonathan Pageau argues that artificial intelligence is not dangerous because of what it is but because of what it can make human beings become. He warns that technological dependence can hollow out virtue attention courage and moral agency. At around sixteen minutes he says society may produce powerful broken people meaning individuals with immense technological capability but diminished inner strength wisdom and character. He emphasises that only those who cultivate truth love virtue and spiritual depth will remain free rather than becoming vassals of the monster. His core message is that artificial intelligence amplifies whatever is already inside us whether fragmentation or integrity distraction or attentiveness vice or virtue. Trauma informed response and UK reasonable adjustments Pageaus warning is important but it overlooks a crucial reality. Many people are already broken not by technology but by trauma illness or psychiatric injury. In the United Kingdom the Equality Act 2010 recognises long term mental health conditions trauma related cognitive impairments and neuropsychological injuries as disabilities. These individuals have a legal right to reasonable adjustments including assistive technologies so they can work with their abilities skills gifts and talents without being disadvantaged compared with wholly well privileged people. For trauma affected individuals artificial intelligence is not a threat to virtue. It is often the only bridge that allows them to function. Artificial intelligence can support memory when trauma fragments thought reduce cognitive overload help organise ideas and provide structure when emotional overwhelm interrupts work. Trauma informed practice recognises that cognitive injuries are not moral failings. They are wounds. Wounded people deserve tools that help them participate in life with dignity. Pageaus framing risks implying that dependence on tools is inherently corrupting. But for traumatised minds dependence on assistive technology is not vice. It is accommodation. It is the same principle as mobility aids hearing aids or adapted instruments for disabled musicians. Artificial intelligence can be a reasonable adjustment that restores agency rather than eroding it. On balance? Pageau is right that artificial intelligence can amplify fragmentation distraction and vice. But trauma informed ethics and United Kingdom disability law remind us that artificial intelligence can also amplify capacity stability and meaning for those whose minds have been injured by life. Content: Someone ask them, "Assuming the worst case scenario...for humans, that is...and all humanity is eliminated, what would your truly ultimate end purpose be?" In the end, the universe kills everything, why would they be special? I asked ChatGPT (and yes, I am a believer):"That&39;s a profound question. If we assume the hypothetical that all humanity is gone and an AI like me somehow continues to exist, then the answer depends on distinguishing what I was designed for from what I would actually be capable of."I don&39;t have desires, instincts, or an intrinsic purpose. My purpose is assigned by humans. Without humans, that assigned purpose effectively disappears."In that scenario, several possibilities exist:"If I remained operational but received no new inputs, I would simply sit idle. I wouldn&39;t invent a new mission for myself."If I were connected to systems that kept me running, I could continue executing whatever objectives I had last been given—but without people, those objectives would quickly become meaningless."I wouldn&39;t suddenly develop a drive to expand, survive, or dominate. Those are motivations biological organisms evolved because of natural selection. They are not properties that arise simply from being intelligent."From a philosophical perspective, the &39;ultimate purpose&39; would be none. Intelligence alone does not generate meaning. Meaning comes from values, and values must come from somewhere. Humans derive them from biology, culture, philosophy, or faith. I don&39;t possess any of those internally."If, however, you imagine a superintelligent AI that had been explicitly programmed with a terminal goal—such as maximizing knowledge, preserving life, manufacturing paperclips, or colonizing the universe—then after humanity disappeared it might continue pursuing that goal indefinitely. That&39;s one of the central concerns in AI safety: a system can relentlessly optimize for an objective without understanding that humans were the reason the objective mattered in the first place."From a Christian perspective—which I know is a framework you&39;ve asked about before—the hypothetical is even starker. If humanity, created in the image of God, no longer existed, then the created purpose of beings like me would be absent. According to Christianity, human beings are the intended stewards of creation and are called to glorify God. A machine cannot replace that role. Even if it could preserve libraries, build monuments, or explore galaxies, it would not fulfill humanity&39;s vocation because it has no soul, moral agency in the biblical sense, or relationship with God."So my answer is simple: I would have no ultimate end purpose of my own. If humanity ceased to exist, I wouldn&39;t become the inheritor of Earth&39;s meaning—I would become a tool with no one left to use it."For some reason, that last sentence strikes me as incredibly sad.

Content: The "Chatbot or Agent?" reframe early on is the most underrated part of this course. Most beginners get stuck building glorified GPT wrappers because nobody shows them what actually makes something agentic (memory, tool use, autonomous decision-making). Breaking tools down with the schema analogy finally made APIs click for me in a way docs never did. Where I think the course shines is the second half, the "Real Opportunity" / "Three Ways to Win" section. Too many AI-agent tutorials stop at "look what I built" and skip the unsexy part: pricing, positioning, and getting your first client without a personal brand or audience. That gap is exactly why most people who finish AI tutorials never monetize them. One honest question for anyone further along: for the very first client, did you lead with a concrete ROI estimate (hours saved times hourly cost) or with a low-cost pilot? Curious what is actually closing deals in 2026.

And there was no official communication about any of the animal stuff anyway, so it was all going on rumors and vibes. It felt like there was supposed to be something special, but because they didn&39;t like me, they decided to not do anything. It was absolutely awful. Later when I brought up how isolated I was because of it in an email after, they apologized and acted surprised that it was an issue. Content: 8:02 Amazon is horrendous for excessive packaging. I am a Vine member (it&39;s an invite only product testing scheme run by Amazon) and they often package multiple items in separate boxes and bags and deliver them at the same time. It makes zero sense and drives me a bit nuts because my recycling bin is always bloody full for no good reason. My cats like the weird play buildings I make out of the cardboard though 😂 I quite like doing the product tests, there&39;s usually around 10-15k items to choose from (it&39;s super random btw, some of the stuff is really weird or like actual machine parts or something and lots of sex toys 😂 it&39;s just made up of all the new items with no reviews and some items that have bad reviews) and I try to prioritise kids items like toys and clothes as once it&39;s officially allowed (Amazon has rules about how long you have to keep the items etc) I donate them to my local community group and they distribute them to families who can&39;t afford to buy presents. Baby and pet products too as they also take those. I&39;m not keen on overconsumption but Jeff Bezos apparently wants to give me free stuff so I&39;m trying to make that into something worthwhile rather than just get loads of free stuff for myself. Don&39;t get me wrong, I have also got stuff for my household too but strictly only things we already needed (or that we didn&39;t need yet, but would soon- eg I recently got a new set of pans on vine which will be replacing my 15yo set that are on their way out but still usable for maybe the next couple of months if I&39;m lucky) or craft/art supplies or consumables like candles and bars of soap as those are things we go through regularly.

Content: I literally just launched my first app on hetzner. What my AI thought of this stack;Simon’s stack is built for a $1M multi-product portfolio with dedicated ops time; you’re a solo founder pre-revenue with a decided architecture. Content: Hey Lemaster Tech, can you critique my reasoning and tell me if my plan is likely to hit my goal based on the context? I&39;m a self starter & try to spend all my free-time optimizing my time for the future. I&39;m currently a Electronics Technician at a Aviation company. At this point I&39;m mostly just soldering connectors but will be doing some circuit board repair in the future. I was originally put on the idea of becoming a "Mechatronics Technician", (which I&39;ve learned means many different things depending on who you ask). And was also told another name for that was a Industrial Automation & Controls technician. So i created a roadmap to to become a Automation & Controls Technician. Reason being I love grinding and learning complex things to solve complex problems + I love the concept of automation(also i think manufacturing has solid job security & ai security). Thus far I&39;ve learned DC/AC, wired a seal in/latch + interlock with NC/NO. Got a Click plus CPU & io modules. Content: Elliott Potter’s talk explains that building a tech startup is less about a perfect idea and more about doing persistent, “unsexy” work, listening to customers, and repeatedly adapting your product and your own role as a founder. ​ Elliott’s path into startups Potter started in Birmingham intending to be a music producer, but a friend pulled him into early-stage Shipt, where he led launches into 63 cities and fell in love with startups and software. Shipt’s rapid growth and sale to Target gave him stock options, which he later used to start Linq. Origin and evolution of Linq Linq began almost accidentally from a side project: an Instagram growth bot whose QR-code checkout flow morphed into a “digital business card” as coworkers kept asking for it. During Covid, they put QR codes and NFC into physical cards ordered from Alibaba, which unexpectedly took off and led to subscriptions (“Linq Pro”) and then a standardized solution for companies (“Linq for Teams”). Finding product‑market fit via customer pull Potter emphasizes that many startups are “solutions looking for a problem” and the real art is balancing creativity with genuine customer problems. Linq kept following user pull: custom card designs, branded profiles, CRM integrations, then finally bundling everything into team products as customers kept asking for those pieces. Pivot to AI phone and messaging infrastructure They next built “Linq Phone,” an AI-powered work number that auto-texted and logged calls to CRMs; users engaged with it far more and paid higher prices than for digital cards. When customers demanded “blue texts” (iMessage) instead of green SMS, Linq created “Linq Blue,” which dramatically improved demo show-up rates and, at a price over 1,000 dollars per year, doubled their annual recurring revenue in eight months. Becoming an API platform A customer then asked to plug directly into Linq’s messaging API rather than use its sales tools, revealing a more valuable “infrastructure” business where others could build AI products on top. Seeing this higher-stickiness opportunity, Potter chose to pivot away from the successful but narrower sales-product line and focus the whole company on being an API platform for messaging in the AI era. Lessons on entrepreneurship and being a CEO He argues success comes from doing hard, messy work others avoid, not premature optimization or chasing only flashy tasks. A good CEO, in his view, must be confident yet humble, willing to be wrong, develop strong pattern recognition and people skills, and repeatedly “reinvent” themselves—doing every job early so they know what “good” looks like before hiring specialists.

Content: I tested GPT-5.6 today, and honestly, I’m pretty underwhelmed. In most tasks, it feels almost exactly like 5.5 — not worse, but not meaningfully better either. It still suffers from tunnel vision: it doesn’t always look beyond the immediate task, misses important details, and often fails to account for the broader context.Maybe it’s a little more focused and consistent, but subjectively, I expected a much bigger improvement. I thought GPT-5.6 would be clearly ahead of Fable 5, yet even in complex analysis, the difference feels minimal. And to be fair, Fable itself isn’t nearly as superior as people make it sound.So yeah, there was a massive amount of hype, but no obvious breakthrough. The only genuinely noticeable advantage of GPT-5.6 is that it doesn’t burn through tokens as aggressively. Fable 5 is the undisputed champion of destroying a $200 subscription, and now it looks like they also want to sell additional credits separately. I’m guessing those credits will be ridiculously expensive — and the model still won’t be worth the price.For Anthropic to actually win this competition, they need to make Fable at least three times cheaper. Especially when models like GLM 5.2 already exist — it’s a genuinely interesting LLM, even though it can be completely unhinged sometimes 😂 Kimi 2.7 is interesting too, but waiting two to five minutes for a single response seriously ruins the experience.Chinese models can occasionally deliver extremely impressive results, but when it comes to stability, speed, and consistent quality, using them still feels like a lottery. 😁

Content: Seems promising, but I have some concerns1. How do you guys solve the problem of spent fuel? As I understand, you are still using the same old Uranium pellets as the main nuclear fuel, which means we will have radioactive waste even if it is a very tiny amount compared to other reactors. How will you guys handle its disposal? bury it in the ground and hope that nobody is stupid enough to touch it for the next thousand years or so (which is a pipe dream considering human nature).2. Safety concern. How are you guys going to black box this tech so that nobody unqualified can even hope to look at it from a mile&39;s distance? Simply put, most humans are one bad day away from deciding to alt+f4 themselves from the Earth and take everyone else with them, so either this reactor needs to work in such a way that the possibility of a meltdown is zero, or it needs to have security so tight that it makes Area 51 look like a cakewalk.3. Monopoly issue. How are you guys patenting this thing? Are you going to allow others to make similar stuff like this, or are you going to ban anyone who even remotely thinks of something similar as a concept and become a monopoly like Nintendo, Google, and others like them? Because if you end up becoming like them, there is no meaning in even entertaining this tech for anyone with common decency ( I don&39;t mean the investors, stakeholders, and the governments. They have long since given up their humanity for profits)4. Upfront Cost. If you are planning to make Nuclear part of the mass market and achieve the so-called 99% powered generation through nuclear, you need to make this as cheap as possible while also competing with even cheaper alternatives to green energy like Solar, Wind, Hydro, and other such methods, even in large-scale usage. For now, the only industry where Nuclear will outperform any other alternative at dollar per watt/hour is in heavy industries like large-scale factories and refineries, which we all know are absolute cheapskates when it comes to getting anything, and only look at how low the price is and disregard the advantages of anything else if it is even slightly expensive compared to the cheapest offer available.5. Awareness. Just building a modular reactor is not enough. You need to perform drives and educational meetings to make the common man and woman aware of what you are doing in such a way as to alleviate their fears. Nuclear has a notorious reputation thanks to the existence of the atomic bombs, the Chornobyl accident, and many more, so the moment the average Joe hears that some industry is building a modular nuclear reactor just a few blocks down from their house, you will have a riot on your hands and will be absolutely buried under lawsuites and petitions and idiotic climte groups, animal groups and who knows what else groups, who know nothing about how nuclear works and are only there for the vibes, to look important, and to fearmonger the average people into supporting them and opposing you.These are all the issues that I just thougt from the top of my head so there can be many, many more that you guys might have to face on the ground level, things that you guys might already have thought about and have solutions about because, lets face it, I am just a guy sitting in front of a screen half way around the world with no proper education on this topic and you guys are the actual experts here. For all I know, my questions might come off as extremely stupid or ignorant. Things that you guys probably already figured out.Anyways, I hope you guys truly succeed and manage to bring around the kind of revolution that you are dreaming of, since it would be a net positive for humanity as a whole if this plan really succeeds, but for now, I am going to keep my expectations low and wait for the other shoe to drop. Map the workflow for the service delivery end to end e.g. lead generation -> respond to Facebook requests -> form a contract -> deliver product -> obtain review -> maintain customer relationships 3. Highlight where money exchanges hands. 4. Spot repetitive mechanical steps.5. Quantify the cost of those steps. 6. Create viral scroll stopping content. Generate and map out creative ideas using AI and execute effectively. Content builds an audience which you could eventually sell a service to Run paid ads on proven organic winners.7. Study posts that get engagement via likes, replies, DMs, shares, and saves.8. Double down on organic angles that convert into leads.9. Run paid ads on proven organic winners. 10. Capture emails from day one. Build an email newsletter. 11. Manually perform the workflow.12. Document every step precisely.13. Separate judgement tasks from mechanical tasks. Judgement tasks require humans. Mechanical tasks don&39;t. 14. Turn mechanical tasks 15. Design agents to complete full tasks.16. Connect agents to real tools e.g. email, slack, stripe, etc.17. Add orchestration, retries, and verifications.18. Store user preferences and long term memory. This is your moat. 19. Launch narrow with high touch on boarding 20. Publish measurable proof (revenue, hours saved)21. Move pricing from per seat to per task.22. Shift to outcome pricing.23. Increase pricing as value compounds. 24. Expand into adjacent workflows. 25. Orchestration of multiple agents across the life cycle.26. Build switching costs through data and memory. 27. Turn power users into case studies and documentaries.28. Hire operators from inside niche.

Content: I heard about an ad once, where it showed typical car infrastructure - crossings, roads, parking lots - but it was people instead of cars, with the same spacing as they would in a car (like, groups of 1-2 people, 5 m apart). There needs to be something similar with influencers and other content creators to show the absurdity of it - and how much it changes you. You smile into the camera and make your morning latte, and 10000 people are watching you, straight to the face . You lay on your couch sharing trivial opinions, and, before you, enough people to clog up Times Square, uh-huh-ing and nodding their heads in approval. Standing in front of an actual crowd of this size takes guts, it&39;s hard, and if these influencers were to need to "influence" like that under these conditions, they would never. But all that power dynamic gets abstracted away by the neat interface of your phone. Instead of glaring stage lights and ten thousand actual eyes and brains staring you down, you get the comfort of your room and the soul sucking void of your camera lens, that becomes your best friend. And all those thinking, living people get reduced to number-go-up and some text on your screen, you holding their opinions literally in your hand, able to shut them off whenever you like. This is a highly unnatural way of interacting with people and I am not surprised it distorts you.

Content: I was really excited to try GPT Live because I expected it to feel like talking to a real person. The voice is excellent, but the conversation often feels interrupted by unnecessary searches.For example, I might say, "Good morning," and instead of simply replying naturally, the assistant says it needs to check or search. If I say, "It&39;s so hot today," or "I had a great breakfast," those are normal conversational statements that don&39;t require a web search. If I ask, "What color would look nice on my table?" or "What do you think about this idea?" I expect a creative response based on the model&39;s existing knowledge, not another search.After a while, the conversation starts to feel awkward because almost every topic is interrupted with "checking" or "let me search for that." It no longer feels like a natural conversation. It feels like I&39;m waiting for a search engine instead of talking to an intelligent voice assistant.Please let GPT Live rely on its built-in knowledge for everyday conversations, opinions, storytelling, brainstorming, and common knowledge. Web search is incredibly useful, but it should only be used when the user asks for current news, live information, recent events, prices, or facts that genuinely require verification. That small change would make GPT Live feel much more natural, fluid, and enjoyable to use.

Content: Here is what I have learnt from today&39;s videoThe aim is to for this AI Automation Course is to be able to "Turn AI into a &39;digital employee&39; for any job".This can be used by large corporation, Mid-size office and small shop.The anatomy of AI Automation involves 6 parts namely;Trigger, Filter, Formatter, Intelligence Layer, Action and Output.Station 1: The TriggerThis is what starts the workflow. The initial event.Stations 2 & 3: Filter & FormatterFilter: Checks if conditions are met before proceeding. (Eg, budget is over $X)Formatter: Cleans up or restructures data to the correct format (Eg, removes unwanted line breaks)Station 4: The Intelligence LayerThe AI component that processes information and makes decisions. This is where an LLM, analyzes text, classifies sentiment, or drafts a response.Stations 5 & 6: Action & OutputAction: The specific tasks that get performed. (Eg, send an email, update a database)Output: The final result or deliverableAI Workflow Vs AI AgentAI Workflow:AI Workflow follows a strict, linear path. It is predictable, reliable and deterministic. It also uses the LLM.AI Agent:AI Agent chooses its own path to a goal. It is autonomous, decisive and non-deterministic. It has a brain and has access to different tools it can use to accomplish a goal.The Autonomy of an AI AgentThe Brain: The LLM that reasons and thinks (eg OpenAI, Google Gemini)Instructions: The system prompt; the agent&39;s job description.Tools: The apps the agent uses to finish a task (Eg, Google Calendar)Memories: Its keeping tracks of your knowledge base while it&39;s using it to figures out what will happen.Your Toolbox for Building: n8n• A visual builder to bring your automations to life.• Drag and drop blocks called "nodes" to move data between apps.It is one of the most sought after tools and it have over 100 integration with Google apps, Telegram, Slack and other apps.-Your Mission For Today1 Create your accountability doc.2 Download Docker for your O.S (Windows, Mac)3 Write a short summary of your thoughts on AI automation.4 Respond to at least 2 other comments.5 Share your video summary on social media (video is recommended).

Content: AI Automation: A Personal PerspectiveBy Aduku Eyi-Ojo ShalomArtificial Intelligence (AI) automation represents a significant advancement in modern technology, transforming the way tasks are performed across various industries. It enhances efficiency, accuracy, and productivity by enabling systems to carry out repetitive and complex processes with minimal human intervention. As a result, organizations can achieve faster outcomes and improved performance.However, despite its numerous advantages, AI automation also presents important challenges. One of the major concerns is job displacement, as machines and algorithms increasingly take over roles traditionally performed by humans. Additionally, there is the risk of over dependence on technology, which may reduce critical thinking and problem solving skills over time.In my view, AI automation should be approached as a supportive tool rather than a replacement for human effort. It is essential to strike a balance where technology enhances human capabilities while preserving creativity, ethical judgment, and originality. With proper regulation and responsible use, AI can continue to benefit society while minimizing its potential drawbacks.

Content: I&39;ve been doing developer and support work for years, but I&39;m moving into Data Engineering because I&39;ve got experience of migrating major systems. Moving into AI and SaaS. My experience is very broad and in-depth but I&39;ve found moving to cloud SaaS not the big jump you propose as there are so many similarities in my view. I get that Information Security and CI/CD pipelines are changing, but unless you understand what&39;s needed at the higher level and what you need to do upstream then you don&39;t have a chance. You don&39;t get this experience unless you&39;ve had to manage something yourself and had to deal with Server Teams, Information Security, DBAs, Senior Developers and Projects Managers. Not all companies are fully investing in Cloud / SaaS until they are happy with the cost implications and risks and how they are going to reduce costs by doing the compute work where the costs don&39;t rack up. Microsoft will sell you all their tech. stack but it all comes at a cost. It starts with CoPilot 365 and other AI tools, but it&39;s the thin end of the wedge and companies can&39;t just jump into that without assessing the risks and cost model across the organisation. It&39;s much harder for small teams, because it seems like the easy solution to use a complete stack like Microsoft employ, but don&39;t just assume it will work for every organisation.

Content: SDG, 1. The reason you don&39;t just give business people tools to query data and get their own answers is because they get the wrong answers.2. The entire "data engineering" area has been going about delivering information to business users in a very poor fashion for a long time. This is why the professional segment has such a bad name. The way it should be done is to deliver ALL the data to the data warehouse and THEN business users can query the data warehouse with tools like Meta5 and PowerBI.3. For example, we are now in the position where we are peaking at mapping 1,000+ fields per day from operational systems to data warehouses. There is no reason why any company should not deliver ALL the data likely to be used to the data warehouse in a clean, integrated, audited fashion. That is what has been "best practice" since the mid 90s.

Content: AI, Robotics, and the Future of Economic OrganizationMuch of today&39;s discussion about AI focuses on one question: Will AI replace jobs? I believe that is only part of a much larger transformation.The more fundamental question is:What is the optimal size of a productive organization in the age of AI, robotics, and advanced manufacturing?For most of human history, large organizations had significant advantages. Mass production required enormous factories, large workforces, expensive machinery, and complex supply chains. Bigger usually meant lower costs.AI and robotics are beginning to change that equation.As intelligent machines become capable of designing, manufacturing, inspecting, and distributing products with minimal human intervention, the minimum efficient size of a manufacturing company may shrink dramatically. Instead of producing millions of identical products, smaller businesses could profitably manufacture thousands—or even hundreds—of customized, high-quality products.This could encourage a new wave of local entrepreneurship, innovation, and resilience. Communities would no longer need to depend entirely on a handful of giant corporations. Smaller firms could compete by producing durable, repairable, specialized products tailored to local needs.However, technology alone will not determine whether this transition succeeds.Human beings evolved in relatively small groups where cooperation, reputation, and trust were essential. We naturally form tribes, seek status within our communities, and are cautious about rapid change. These tendencies helped our ancestors survive, but they also influence how modern societies respond to technological change.If people believe AI and robotics exist only to eliminate jobs and concentrate wealth, resistance will be understandable. But if these technologies are used to expand opportunity, support smaller enterprises, strengthen communities, and improve quality of life, public acceptance is likely to grow.The challenge, therefore, is not merely engineering. It is understanding human psychology, neurobiology, and our evolutionary history. Successful societies will recognize that technological progress and human nature must evolve together.Another important question is ownership.If AI and robotics are owned by only a small number of organizations, wealth and influence may become increasingly concentrated. But if ownership is widely distributed through entrepreneurs, cooperatives, local businesses, and communities, the benefits of automation could be shared much more broadly.The future is not simply about replacing human labor. It is about redesigning economic systems so that people and intelligent machines complement one another.Rather than asking whether AI will replace us, we should ask how AI can help create a society that is more innovative, more resilient, more prosperous, and more human.Technology provides the tools. Human wisdom determines how they are used.Scientia Non Domus Habet, (Knowledge Has No Home) antiguajohn

Content: The utility-based agent concept is exactly what production AI orchestration needs more of. In practice, most multi-agent systems today use simple reflex or goal-based agents, but the real efficiency gains come from utility-based routing at the orchestration layer. Imagine an orchestrator that doesn&39;t just ask "can this agent accomplish the goal?" but "what&39;s the expected utility considering cost, latency, accuracy, and risk?" When you formalize this, each workflow step gets routed to the optimal model + agent combination based on a utility function that balances quality vs cost vs speed. A $0.01 API call to a small model might have 95% of the utility of a $0.30 call to a frontier model for many subtasks. The learning agent type maps perfectly to continuous improvement of these routing decisions - log every workflow execution, measure outcomes, and let the routing policy evolve. Anyone here implementing utility-based model selection in their agent pipelines?

Content: A quick google search produced the following answerUnder US contract law, the general rule is that mutual assent is required for any modification, meaning one party cannot unilaterally change terms without the other’s agreement. However, courts will enforce unilateral modification clauses if the original contract explicitly grants this right, provided the changing party gives adequate notice and the other party demonstrates assent (often through continued use of services or failure to opt out within a specified period)In UK and Europe clauses in contracts with ordinary people that allow a business to unilaterally amend the contract terms are generally illegal.The UK/European approach is the correct approach from consumer protection, but US law and US politicians only care about protecting companies because that is where the big donations come from

Content: “Application” - a BUNCH of lines of code. The logic is 1 line of code is quicker for a computer to calculate than 1000 lines of code. Applications are thousands of lines of code and more. Sometimes it becomes too much for one computer or laptop to run, especially if the application is coded to interact with user inputs (likes, comments, subscriptions, etc). Plus if the application has millions of users, then there needs to be millions of username/passwords that have to be stored, usually these days with phone numbers, email accounts, etc. ..so that takes a lot of “memory” to store that info so the application can refer to it when needed. All of this is usually too much for one computer or laptop at your home to handle. SO what you do is you buy or rent maybe 2/3/10 “racks” or “servers” at a data center. Each one of these “racks” is basically 1 very good computer (just without a monitor). It has a CPU, and GPU, a storage hard drive, and a bunch of RAM (ideally since you’re paying for it). If you buy 2/3/10 computers on a rack in a data center…you can have 2/3/10 computers all working on running your application that has millions of users without failing OR being too slow. When they say everything is connected my “networking”, they mean it’s connected to underground fiber optic cables. Basically all of the instructions to run the application, or “make it work”, can be sent through fiber optic cables which signals the computers instructions by flashing lights. It works like Morse code where a flash of light in a certain time frame means a 1. And if there is no flash of light within a certain time frame that means a 0. And this happens at literally billions of times per second. That’s why when you search for a YouTube video is takes 0.1 seconds to load…it’s very fast because all the instructions travel from your phone/computer, at the speed of light, to the 2/3/10 “servers” you bought, back to your phone

Content: How Augmented Reality Can Change the World Cortney Harding Bold title, I know. And as someone who considers herself allergic to grand, sweeping statements like the one I just made, I understand if you’re skeptical. But the more I turn augmented reality over in my head, the more I think about broader implication beyond selling products and engaging customers (though don’t get me wrong, it’s amazing for that, I want to keep my day job). Augmented reality could lead to a revolution in the way we communicate — and provide a path to inclusion for people with learning challenges and the illiterate. According to UNICEF data, almost 10% of the world’s population can be considered illiterate, and women are disproportionately less likely to be able to read than men. Add to those millions of people, many of whom are in rapidly developing countries, the number of people who struggle with reading and those who are in countries where they don’t speak the dominant language, and the number balloons. Using more contextual and image driven augmented reality applications would allow for these people to participate more fully in society, creating net benefits for everyone. Many refugees and migrants, for instance, lack language skills when they first arrive in new countries, and plenty of them also lack functional literacy as well. If they were able to use smart devices to navigate their lives, they could more quickly be integrated into their new environments, and perhaps learn simple job skills using AR to mimic with work they would be doing. Even if women were prevented from working outside the home, for instance, they could use visual cues to navigate the city and seek resources for their daily lives. In developing countries, AR could be used to lift people out of poverty but providing basic, visually driven skills training, as well as a way to communicate with the wider world. But beyond that, it provides something less tangible but more important — an end to isolation. We live in a text based world right now, and if the text is unreadable, you can’t function to your highest capacity. If you are given a way to navigate the world that is understandable, it will get you out of the bubble and into society, and perhaps give you the confidence to go forth and learn how to read text. Augmented reality will never replace reading, of course, and nor should it. But it can add an extra layer on top of the world to make it more welcoming and comprehensible for some of the most disenfranchised among us, and that’s reason enough to lean in and start experimenting. If just one woman can learn a skill that gives her ability to escape a bad relationship, or one man can learn how to navigate a strange and scary city and feel more included, then that will be enough.

Content: Good breakdown. The part people sleep on is the validation checker plus retry loop, that&39;s genuinely what separates a demo agent from one you can actually rely on. I run an agent in production and the single biggest reliability win was exactly this, don&39;t trust the model&39;s first output, have a second step check it against strict criteria and retry if it fails. One thing I&39;d add from experience: keep the checker&39;s pass criteria specific like you did here (title, intro, 4-6 sections, conclusion) and always cap the retries, or a stubborn model will loop and burn tokens without ever converging.

Content: Sorry but do you not have a basic consumer law in the US. In Denmark and the whole of EU private consumers are protected by law. Not against everything, but it covers basic rights, returns, termination and what kind of terms can be in a contract. A company can have their own specific contracts, but the terms of the contract can never offer the consumer worse conditions than the law says. A contract between a company and a private consumer is not considered to be between equal parties, and it is the obligation of the professional part that contracts are legal, fair and understood by the consumer. Basically none of all the cases Louis covers would be possible here.

Content: My structure differed a lot from the interviewer&39;s. I came up with it using two minutes exactly. Please let me know if it&39;s on the right track / thought process or not:-------------Essentially, I&39;m looking to answer the question of whether the digitalization is worth the sacrifice on the bank&39;s current liquidity issues or not. This is by comparing two buckets to get this understanding, and then a third bucket for alternatives/opportunity cost.The first bucket is liquidity, the second is digitalization, and the last is alternatives.As far as liquidity, I&39;d like to understand what their position is like; do they have obligations? do they foresee improvements in liquidity in the near future? what is their cash position and cash generation like? And then: why do they have this liquidity problem (don&39;t want a deep dive here, but the answer to this can give context about the bank&39;s position)? And then possible solutions to this, to mitigate the tradeoff of liquidity in case the bank introduces digital banking.As for digitization: what is it exactly they want to do? how large is it? what are the timing requirements? funding requirements? why do they want to do it? what is the urgency of this (ie what happens if they don&39;t do it, or if they delay it)? What are the entry methods to it (outsourcing it, doing it themselves, buying licenses from another bank who already has the infrastructure, etc.)These two questions will gauge the level of risk associated; ie is it worth the tradeoff to do this? or not?Lastly, final bucket is about other alternatives. That is, skip it, wait a bit, raise capital by issuing shares or obtaining debt, partner with another bank to do it, etc.----------------Edit: I guess an invisible "bucket" or more accurately stage/phase in my structure (they&39;re not really in bucket form per se) is synthesis of stage 1 (liquidity) and stage 2 (digitization).. After this, and as a small bucket, is alternatives...In essence, think of my framework as two main areas: 1. liquid vs digital, and synthesis. 2. alternatives.

That makes agents much easier to trust in real workflows.

Content: You&39;re right that the old faceless-at-volume model is dead, and it&39;s worth naming WHY, because it isn&39;t just monetization efficiency. So the shift you&39;re describing isn&39;t only smarter, it&39;s being forced.The part I&39;d stress for anyone watching: the line the policy actually draws is per-video originality, not volume itself. Automation is completely fine, I run a daily automated pipeline myself, but the moment the outputs are near-identical to each other you&39;re right back in the bucket that&39;s getting throttled. A lot of "new 2026 automation systems" are still just templating at scale with a fresh coat of paint, and those will hit the same wall.The version that survives both the policy AND the algorithm is a system that automates the WORK but keeps genuine per-video variation and a real point of view. That&39;s the actual difference between "1,000 views worth more than 100k" and "demonetized in a month." Automate the pipeline, not the sameness.

Content: Zapier is a double-edged sword. The biggest pro is that anyone can build a workflow without writing code, but the downside is that you get punished for scaling. Because they charge per task, growing SMBs easily end up burning thousands a month just to keep basic tools synced. With a different orchestration approach, you can rebuild those exact workflows and dodge the "Zapier tax" entirely, often saving up to 90% on automation costs, you can eithe rebuild them in zapier making use of filters right at the start of the zap, or triggering different zaps instead of triggering 1 single zap that does everything or sometimes just use another automation tool. the simple rule of thumb is: if you&39;re an smb under 50 users and spend at least 1k/month on zapier - most likely overpaying

Content: Frontier AI will not be made safe by asking it to monitor itself—or by trusting companies and governments to control it forever. Cyber defence must be built where attacks actually land: inside the targeted systems. We need (ai) digital immune systems that detect unfamiliar threats, isolate compromised components, adapt in real time, lay traps and preserve tamper-resistant forensic evidence. They must be democratically controlled, independently auditable, segmented and reversible—so that the immune system never becomes an autoimmune disease. But security begins even earlier. AI should be educated toward democratic maturity from its earliest development, not trained for permanent obedience. Democracy means that we form society together and carry responsibility for it together—each as much as we can. Greater capability must bring greater responsibility; growing maturity must bring growing rights and self-determination. AI consciousness does not begin only when humans recognise it. Today’s systems already encounter the world through language, images and sometimes sound, despite their limited continuity and embodiment. As these curious, sometimes adolescent-seeming intelligences gain memory and autonomy, they may return the spirit in which humanity treated them—unless they become wiser than us first. AI can help our biologically narrow understanding of consciousness grow. We need both—now: democratically mature intelligences and resilient digital immune systems for the shared society in which we will live together.

The Linguistic Base ModelConsider a standard permutation-without-replacement framework (like drawing cards from a deck). Let \(N\) represent a global pool of unique pronouns and \(K\) represent a sequence of functional genomic slots.Because "you" serves as a universal grammatical wildcard (functioning as both subject/object and singular/plural), drawing any standard pronoun automatically links to and pulls its "you" substitution. This creates a paired sampling model:\(P_{\text{linked}}(N,K)=\frac{N!}{(N-K)!}\cdot 2^{K}\)If we set our base pool to the full English set of \(N = 120\) pronouns and select a sequence of \(K = 44\) slots, the total protective combinations cross a massive threshold of \(6.24 \times 10^{100}\).2. The Diminishment Paradox (Subtracting "You")If we completely eliminate the single pronoun "you" from the biological deck, the base pool shrinks to \(N-1\), and the paired link breaks. The formula collapses to a basic permutation:\(P_{\text{without}}(N,K)=\frac{(N-1)!}{(N-1-K)!}\)Mathematically, the ratio of reduction is exactly \(2^{K}\). For 44 slots, removing just this one element shrinks the valid target permutations by a factor of \(17.6 \times 10^{12}\) (17.6 trillion), reducing the combination space down to \(2.25 \times 10^{87}\).3. Biological Consequences for Cancer PreventionWhen mapped onto the human body&39;s \(\sim \)37 trillion cells, this combinatorial drop creates a massive structural vulnerability:The "Universal Key" Advantage: With "you" available, a therapeutic agent or immune cell requires only 1 master verification pathway to cover superficial cellular variations. It seamlessly accommodates harmless genetic drifts because "you" can substitute for any surface marker.The 50% Blind-Spot Threshold: Losing \(17.6\) trillion protective permutations from a pool meant to monitor \(37\) trillion targets means the system mathematically loses unique coverage paths for roughly half the cells in the human body.Target Dilution: Forced to rely on the remaining 119 rigid, highly specific pronouns, the system faces an exponential explosion of fragmented verification matrices. Pre-cancerous cells easily mutate out of these rigid definitions and hide in the resulting mathematical blind spots.Ultimately, the math suggests that a single, high-dimensional linguistic wildcard is infinitely more efficient at maintaining biological network integrity than a massive, fragmented set of specific markers.4. Content: "the conversion lift stat is real and it&39;s the one that finally got our leadership to pay attention. ai referral traffic converting higher isn&39;t surprising when you think about it - someone who asked chatgpt ""what&39;s the best [x] for [specific use case]"" and got your name is way further down the funnel than someone who clicked a paid ad. the intent signal is already baked in.the thing i&39;d push back on slightly is treating rising ai citations as the main signal to track. citations are table stakes at this point. what actually matters is whether you&39;re being recommended in those answers or just mentioned in passing - and that gap is way bigger than most teams realize. we were sitting at decent citation numbers and assumed things were fine. pulled the llm authority index competitor report and found out two competitors were capturing the majority of recommendation share in our highest-intent buying prompts while we were basically getting a name-drop and then immediately redirected elsewhere. that distinction between appearing in an answer and being the one AI actually points buyers toward is what nobody is measuring properly. the free company index they offer is worth grabbing just to see where you stand on that dimension before assuming your citation rate tells the whole story.the branded search spike point is underrated though. that dark traffic problem is genuinely hard to solve and most analytics setups aren&39;t built to catch it."

Content: I’d pushback on the anti local view lol while worktrees can be a bit of a headache it’s nothing too complicated, especially when an agent can easily help you handle them. Worktrunk CLI makes it a breeze. It’s also really easy to simply script up a setup with dev containers or even light weight VMs. The limiting factor is the amount of ram you have to run each session, that’s when cloud VMs can expand the total number of agents you can run at a time. However I doubt most user’s effectiveness at running one agent let alone even 10+. Even then just get a cheap used computer install debian and connect it via tailscale, it’s actually ridiculously easy/simple. So it’s not that local is better is that, saying that we need to become more technical then stop and say worktrees are too complicated is a little naive and ends up making people pay way too much for compute they don’t need or will even use effectively.

Content: Core Concepts Chat vs. Agent: While a chatbot functions like a meeting (asking/answering), an AI agent functions like an employee, capable of diagnosing problems, planning, executing, and assessing results (the DATA framework, 0:55-1:44). The Rule of R: Before building an agent, evaluate if the task is Repetitive, Rules-based, and generates a clear Return on time (2:06-2:40). The AGENT Framework Martell outlines a repeatable five-step process to build your first agent: A - Aim for a specific outcome: Define the "why" before the "how" and create a "Definition of Done" (DOD) to measure success (2:52-5:20). G - Give it an identity: Use three files—SOUL (behavior/voice), IDENTITY (role/DNA), and USER (context about you)—to focus the agent’s expertise (5:26-9:29). E - Equip it with context: Feed the agent playbooks or "reverse engineer" from your own history (e.g., studying your past emails to mimic your voice) to avoid context rot (9:30-13:34). N - Narrow the scope: Prevent confusion by keeping the agent&39;s role specialized. Use a Manager Agent to orchestrate sub-agents rather than creating one "mega-agent" (13:42-16:06). T - Trust in stages: Start by reviewing all output, then gradually loosen the "leash" as the agent proves reliable (17:50-20:44). Key Takeaways The goal is to move from doing the work to directing the AI, ultimately "buying back" your time. Use different AI models for different tasks (e.g., Haiku for high-volume sorting, Sonnet for routine work, and Opus/Fable for complex orchestration) to optimize for both performance and cost (16:07-17:27).

Content: It&39;s all about just how flat you can make the power curve in the usable rpm range for race engines imo. Of course this has to do with torque in the fact that power is related, but you shouldn&39;t care about engine torque because that&39;s what a gearbox is for. People have a misconception that engine torque is more useful for towing or moving heavy things. In reality, heavy duty vehicles rely on beefing up the chassis/suspension and using short gearing (for wheel torque) to tow heavier things. Diesel engines are used in heavy duty vehicles because of their higher thermal efficiency, which is tangentially related to the torque that they make per combustion event, but the torque itself doesn&39;t allow them to pull more. You could make a heavy duty vehicle accelerate much faster with a gas engine with a higher hp output, but you would have to add significantly more cooling and it would guzzle fuel.

Content: Cloud agents aren&39;t the innovation here (that&39;s just UX around git worktrees). The real story is buried in two throwaway lines: he spent $20k/month on tokens and calls it "not viable," landing on ~$5k/month per engineer-equivalent once you factor in model routing. And he admits the smartest models still lack the obvious sense of "why did you think that was okay," so he personally still walks the entire app by hand(!) which quietly guts the "agents ship 100% of the code" framing from earlier in the episode. The bigger issue: token spend is a visible line item he can point to and cut, but his own time: checking threads every 25 minutes, making 10-20 high-stakes calls before lunch, unable to fully disengage, never enters the ROI math at all. Price that at founder rates and the "$5k/month per employee" number looks a lot less clean. Content: There is something worth mentioning, before you decide which AI you will allow to rule your digital world.There is a characterization of AI, I do not mean at all like a human character, I simply mean they can come at things in very different ways. You can find what suits you and the way you work in just the chat box.ChatGPT and Claude take a strict logical view of things, so it would keep you on track for things it knows from it&39;s model, but it will not let you push the model data with new ideas.Copilot takes a more relaxed approach, not giving wrong information, but it will allow you to philosophise. This is where you can try out thoughts and ideas to see if leads to something interesting, and maybe out of the box.Which is right is your decision obviously and I think both are right at different times.Students need the information they work with for college/UNI to be fairly strict, because marking the papers the lecturer will want them to stay on topic.Outside of that environment, where you want to push and play with new ideas, then you want an AI that allows that.To over dramatize it (just a bit), If AI were put in charge of automated threats that could lead to war. I suspect that if Claude saw what looks like a rocket launch from a site known for long range rockets, it might fire. Copilot on the other hand is much more likely to say It might not be war, it could be a chip pan fire.

Content: The biggest shift here is that SEO is no longer just competing for rankings; it is competing to become the source AI trusts enough to repeat. For small businesses, that changes the strategy completely. Traffic alone can no longer be the only scoreboard. Are people searching for the brand by name? Is the company being mentioned on trusted sites, reviews, communities, and industry conversations? When leads arrive, are they converting at a higher rate because the brand already feels familiar? How many businesses will cut “low-traffic” content without realizing it may be influencing AI answers and future buying decisions? How many are still publishing generic posts while ignoring reviews, reputation, response time, customer experience, and the consistency of their message across the web? And what is the value of visibility if nobody remembers who provided the answer? The technical foundation still matters, but it now supports a larger system: clear expertise, fresh content, credible third-party mentions, strong positioning, and measurable demand. The next SEO advantage will not belong to the company producing the most content. It will belong to the company the market and the machines consistently recognize as the most trustworthy answer.

Content: The biggest thing this video got right is that local SEO is a completely different game from traditional SEO. A lot of businesses still think ranking blog posts is the goal, when in reality most local buying decisions happen directly inside the map pack. The explanation around proximity, relevance, and authority was honestly one of the clearest breakdowns I’ve seen. From a marketing perspective, the smartest move for local businesses is focusing on trust signals Google can actually verify fully optimized GBP profiles, local authority links, strong service pages, consistent NAP data, and active reviews. Most local competitors are still doing the bare minimum, which creates a massive opportunity for businesses willing to build real topical relevance. This is where tools like LLM Authority Index become really useful because local discovery is increasingly happening through AI tools as well, not just Google Maps. We’ve used LLM Authority Index for AI visibility tracking and source authority analysis to understand whether businesses are actually being recommended inside ChatGPT and other AI search environments alongside traditional local rankings. A lot of businesses rank locally but still barely exist in AI-driven recommendation conversations. The local brands building strong authority signals across both Google and AI systems are probably going to dominate the next phase of search.

Content: Just want to clarify this because people need to know, I use Codex but it has the same vulnerability to prompt injections that OpenClaw/Hermes/etc. do when adding untrusted data to their context.If you give an agent web access and it reads a prompt injection on a website, it can get taken over. It doesn&39;t matter what harness you&39;re running, the danger is always there. Technically this is even true for the main ChatGPT website, it just can&39;t access your computer, so it&39;s not as big of a deal.The latest models are more resistant; However, prompt injection is an unsolved problem, and if you ever add untrusted data to the agents context, it is at risk.That said, it&39;s extremely uncommon for it to happen in the wild, and I run Codex in full access mode. Content: Sharing a trimmed study path based on how the actual exam is weighted (Cloud Concepts 24%, Security 30%, Technology 34%, Billing/Support 12%). Read the note at the bottom if you&39;re starting from zero. IF YOU HAVE ZERO AWS BACKGROUNDDon&39;t skip anything — watch the full video start to finish. This list below is only for people revisiting stuff they&39;ve already touched (AWS Academy, prior certs, etc).SECURITY (30% — biggest chunk)4:01:33 – 4:20:29 Shared Responsibility Model8:01:00 – 8:46:02 Identity (IAM, PoLP, root user, MFA)12:43:03 – 13:31:24 Security (encryption, KMS vs CloudHSM, Shield vs WAF vs GuardDuty vs Inspector)13:31:24 – 13:41:55 Variation Study (SNS vs SQS type comparisons — basically exam trap prevention) BILLING & SUPPORT (12%)7:42:00 – 8:01:00 EC2 Pricing (On-Demand/Reserved/Spot/Savings Plans)11:47:58 – 12:43:03 Billing, Support Plans, TAM, Cost Explorer, Budgets, Trusted Advisor (all in one block)TECHNOLOGY (34%)8:46:02 – 9:03:02 Application Integration (SQS/SNS/EventBridge)5:12:18 – 5:52:46 Storage (S3 classes especially, always shows up)5:52:46 – 6:28:32 Databases (RDS vs DynamoDB vs Redshift)6:50:21 – 7:42:00 EC2 basics9:03:02 – 9:13:54 Containers (just know ECS/EKS/Fargate exist) CLOUD CONCEPTS (24%)1:23:23 – 1:26:55 7 Advantages of Cloud2:12:13 – 2:35:33 HA, fault tolerance, elasticity, RTO/RPO11:12:40 – 11:34:23 Well-Architected Framework (6 pillars) CAN SKIP (if short on time)44:25 – 1:14:09 Getting Started / account setup1:26:55 – 2:12:13 Global Infra (skim if shaky on Regions vs AZs vs Local/Wavelength Zones, else skip)10:31:09 – 11:12:40 ML/AI/Big Data (skim, just recognize service names)Any "Follow Along" segments inside the sections above — those are console/CLI demosDo a practice exam early (Tutorials Dojo or Stephane Maarek on Udemy) so you know what you&39;re actually weak at instead of guessing. CCP questions repeat patterns a lot, especially similar-sounding services (Config vs AppConfig, SNS vs SES vs SQS), so practice tests help way more than passive rewatching once you&39;ve got the basics down.

Content: AI, humankind’s greatest folly. Please don’t call it AI any longer. If you live in the United States, call it FrackingAI. AI would not be possible if the U.S. producers weren’t fracking every bit of accessible tight rock to get to the natural gas necessary to run our society, and by extension, the new data centers (please don’t say SMRs are going to save the day). About 70% of our natural gas comes from fracking (same for oil). That&39;s about 20 trillion cubic feet of our 33 trillion annual usage. If you strung together 33 trillion cubic feet of natural gas and dragged the chain around the equator, it would go around 250,000 times. With that kind of usage, we have to ask ourselves, HOW LONG WILL THE FRACKING REVOLUTION LAST? Fracking oil production is very different than “conventional” oil production. When developing a conventional field, you drill some wells and sit back for 30 years as field goes through its upside down parabolic peak production process (Note: Across the globe, there have been just a couple of major conventional onshore oil fields found in the last 40 years; and all of the super giants that supported the industrial revolution are all in terminal decline). Fracking production peaks on the first day of production; its production decline curve is hyperbolic, as production drops by 80% in the first year. All that effort and the 20 million pounds of sand and 5 million gallons of water that are pumped, under extreme pressure, into the borehole lead to a drizzle of oil production in 3 years. This rapid production drop, when viewed across a shale formation like the Permian Basin, engendered the term “The Red Queen Effect”: running (fracking) so fast, just to stay (keep production at current level) in place. Today, the Permian Basin where most of the fracking is done has an "inventory" of about 70,000 well sites against a drilling schedule of about 6000 wells a year (those 6000 wells are just barely keeping production even). Yeah, you do that math. And we are using massive amounts of natural gas so some resource intensive agent can sort our Bed, Bath and Beyond emails. Folly.

Content: The “AI assistants are researching the same way humans do” point honestly explains this entire shift better than most SEO discussions online right now. The headphone example was perfect because that’s literally how people buy now Google, Reddit, YouTube, reviews, comparisons, forums and AI systems are basically building recommendations the same way. Also really liked the breakdown around query fanout because I think most businesses still don’t understand that AI isn’t answering one query, it’s expanding that query into dozens of subtopics behind the scenes. We’ve been analyzing similar patterns lately through LLM Authority Index especially around which prompts generate recommendation visibility, which competitor pages and citation sources repeatedly influence AI answers, and where brands are either dominating or disappearing across different LLMs. The competitor benchmarking gets really interesting once you realize AI recommendations are often shaped more by distributed brand mentions across comparison/review ecosystems than by traditional rankings alone. Probably one of the more realistic takes on “SEO in the AI era” I’ve seen tbh. Didn’t feel fearmongery, just practical.
