Content: 📢 Google將NotebookLM改名為Gemini Notebook Google於美國時間7月16日正式宣布，將旗下人工智能研究工具NotebookLM改名為Gemini Notebook，此舉屬品牌整合，並非推出全新產品，用戶原有筆記、資料及功能將完整保留。Google在官方部落格表示，Gemini Notebook仍將維持獨立產品定位，繼續作為用戶研究的首選工具，但未來會在Google整體生態系統中扮演更重要角色，包括與Gemini應用程式及Google搜尋作更深度整合。 🕰️ 品牌統一背後的發展歷程 Gemini Notebook前身NotebookLM於2023年以「Project Tailwind」為代號啟動，並在當年Google I/O大會首度亮相，定位為協助整理及理解資料的研究助手。同年7月起開放候補名單申請，隨後率先於美國推出，並逐步擴展至全球市場，功能亦不斷擴充。此次改名後，介面標誌亦換上與Gemini系列一致的藍紫漸層設計，以配合Google整體人工智能品牌形象。 🔗 維持獨立產品定位 儘管更名，Gemini Notebook並不會被併入Gemini聊天機械人主體，而是繼續以獨立研究工具形式運作，惟兩者之間的內容將可同步使用。有外媒指出，由於Gemini應用程式本身亦已具備筆記本功能，故此次整合或會令部分用戶對兩者關係感到混淆，但Google強調兩個版本的筆記本是互相連結及同步的。Google方面預告，未來Gemini Notebook的內容將逐步整合至Google搜尋的AI模式（AI Mode），惟暫未公布具體時間表。 💻 新增雲端運算及分析功能 除品牌更名外，Google亦為Gemini Notebook引入代號為「安全雲端電腦」的新功能，讓用戶可直接在筆記本內編寫及執行程式碼，進行更深入的資料分析工作，例如根據上傳文件生成統計摘要。此項功能率先向Google AI Ultra及Workspace商業版用戶開放，Google表示將於未來數周內逐步擴展至網頁版AI Pro用戶，並支援更多輸出格式。 📈 使用規模龐大 涵蓋教育及企業界 根據Google公布數字，Gemini Notebook（前稱NotebookLM）目前已錄得超過3,000萬名使用者，以及逾60萬個機構或組織使用，應用範圍涵蓋學生課堂筆記整理，以至企業新員工入職培訓資料製作。工具核心功能包括自動生成資料摘要，以及根據使用者提供的內容製作音訊與視訊概述，協助用戶更有效率地消化及傳遞知識。 ✅ 對現有用戶影響輕微 多家科技媒體分析指出，此次更動對一般用戶而言學習成本極低，因原有筆記本內容、功能及操作方式基本維持不變，系統將自動重新導向，確保現有共用連結及筆記本正常運作。Google Workspace更新頁面亦指出，管理員無需採取任何行動，新名稱及標誌將於未來數星期內，透過網頁及流動應用程式版本逐步向全球用戶推出。 內容由 AI Marketer HK 製作 ———— 👇 相信「AI × 數碼營銷」是未來的你， 歡迎 Tag 一位同行好友，一起成長！ AIMarketerHK DigitalMarketing Gemini GeminiNotebook NotebookLM

Content: Tens of thousands of AI prompts. Now running on Microsoft's own model. Microsoft just quietly redirected a massive chunk of its AI workload in Excel and Outlook away from OpenAI and Anthropic, routing it through its own in-house MAI models instead. The reason? Microsoft's AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman put it plainly: the goal is to "reduce and ultimately eliminate" the cost of paying third-party AI providers. This is the build-vs-buy question playing out in real time, at the largest scale possible. Every enterprise that has woven third-party AI APIs into its workflows is carrying a version of this risk: dependency on vendors whose pricing, availability, and priorities are outside your control. Microsoft had the runway to build its way out. Most organisations don't. But the question it raises is worth putting on the table: how embedded are you in any single AI vendor's ecosystem, and what does your contingency look like if that changes? Content: I used to ship 2-3 features a week. Now it is 2-3 a day. Same models. Same codebase. Same developer. Here is what changed. Every session with an AI agent started from zero. It did not know my architecture, my design system, or my rules. So it built things that looked right and were wrong. Wrong folder, wrong pattern, hardcoded strings that should have been translation keys, no tests. I spent more time correcting it than the work would have taken me. The model was never the problem. I was asking a capable engineer to work on a large codebase with no onboarding, and doing it again every morning. So I stopped, and I built the onboarding. Docs written for agents instead of humans. A memory directory the agent writes to itself, so what it learns survives the session. Then seven custom Claude Code skills, one per workflow. Entry point, new features, testing, localization, git commits, hydration, docs and memory sync. The entry point is the one that changed everything. Every task starts there. It reads the rules, opens the memory index, loads only the docs that task needs, then routes to the rest. But my favorite part is not a skill. It is a hook. A Stop hook checks whether code changed without docs or memory changing with it. If it did, it blocks the agent from ending the turn. The agent is not allowed to say done. That is not a line in a README nobody reads. It is a shell script. The workflow now: Opus 4.8 plans it, Sonnet 5 subagents build it, Opus reviews them, a code-reviewer skill checks for bugs and security, then I read every line. Opus is expensive. Sonnet is not. Planning is where the expensive model earns its money. Typing is not. Everyone has the same models. Content: SaaS metrics are dead. OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar just published a new framework for measuring AI ROI, and it challenges the foundational metric of the last 20 years: user seat licenses. Since AI performs the actual work—rather than just assisting humans—measuring user adoption is the wrong target. Instead, Friar proposes a new North Star: "Useful Intelligence per Dollar." Here is the 4-pillar scorecard OpenAI uses to track AI value: 1. Task completion effectiveness: Does the AI actually finish the job? (e.g., customer tickets resolved, code changes shipped). 2. Cost per successful task: The total economic efficiency of achieving a successful outcome—not just the raw cost per token. 3. Dependability: Can users rely on the results? (This accounts for retries, error recovery, and human oversight). 4. Value scalability: Does the investment produce more value as usage grows, without costs spiraling out of control? The true price of AI includes the cost of failures. A cheaper, less dependable model that requires human intervention or five retries is actually more expensive than a premium frontier model that succeeds on the first try. Stop counting tokens. Start measuring outcomes. Read the full framework: openai.com/index/a-scorecard-for-the-ai-age — If you're here for signal—not hype—you're in the right place. Content: 🔥 Mozilla's first State of Open Source AI report just dropped and the numbers hit hard. Open models trail closed ones by 3.3 percentage points on benchmarks but handle 33% of production tokens while capturing only 4% of revenue. Think about that gap. You're running inference, paying compute costs, shipping real traffic on open weights. And the money still flows to closed labs charging roughly 6x more per call for comparable quality. Operational costs for open models fell 50x in three years, yet only 51% of teams using open weights actually reach production compared to 63% on closed models. The performance gap isn't what's blocking you. It's deployment tooling. Mistral hit $400M ARR growing twentyfold in 12 months. Databricks is at $5.4B. The commercial layer is real. My agency routes high-volume workloads to open models whenever the task doesn't need advanced reasoning. And the savings are immediate. Audit where your tokens actually go this week. You're probably paying closed prices for work an open model already handles. Content: Connecting enterprise systems doesn't have to mean writing thousands of lines of integration code. That's where Apache Kafka Connect transforms modern data engineering. Instead of building and maintaining custom pipelines, Kafka Connect offers ready-to-use source and sink connectors for databases, REST APIs, cloud storage, search engines, and enterprise applications. Key benefits: Integrate databases like MySQL, PostgreSQL, and Oracle Connect cloud platforms such as AWS S3 and Azure services Stream data from REST APIs and third-party applications Enable scalable, fault-tolerant data pipelines Configure integrations with simple JSON instead of custom code Support both real-time streaming and batch workloads Maintain schema consistency using Schema Registry Whether you're building ETL pipelines, event-driven microservices, IoT platforms, analytics systems, or data lakes, Kafka Connect dramatically reduces development effort while improving reliability and scalability. Understanding Kafka Connect is an essential skill for every modern Data Engineer, Backend Developer, and Cloud Architect working with real-time data ecosystems. Content: Most people think great content is all about using the right keywords. It isn't. The best-performing content is written for people first and optimized for search engines second. Over the years, I've learned that small improvements in your writing style can make a huge difference in rankings, engagement, and conversions. Here's what actually works: 1- Hook people in the first 2 lines. If you don't, they scroll. Simple as that. 2- Answer the main question immediately. Don't make people wait for the "good part." 3- Keep your paragraphs short. One idea per line. Nobody's reading a wall of text on their phone. 4- Use bullet points. They're scannable. They save time. People love that. 5- Break the pattern sometimes. Say something unexpected. Surprise your reader mid-post. 6- Write like you're talking to ONE person. Not a crowd. Not an audience. One human being. 7- Cut the fluff. If a sentence doesn't add value, delete it. No mercy. 8- Make your FAQs actually useful. Not the generic ones everyone copies. 9- Add a quick summary box. Some people just want the TL;DR. Give it to them. 10- And always, always end with something actionable. Give people a next step. Great content doesn't just rank—it builds trust, solves problems, and converts readers into customers. Content: 🌻Same Architecture. New Substrate. What if an LLM Agent is not as fundamentally different from a computer as we think? Look closely at a traditional computer: 🧠 CPU → performs computation 🧮 RAM → holds working information 💾 Hard Disk → stores information long-term 🔌 Device Drivers → connect the system to external hardware ⚙️ Operating System → coordinates everything 🖥️ Application → uses all these layers to perform useful tasks Now map that architecture to an LLM Agent: 🧠 LLM / Model Weights → the reasoning engine 📄 Context Window → working memory 🗄️ Vector DB / Long-term Storage → persistent knowledge 🔧 Tool Integrations → access to external systems and capabilities ⚙️ Agent Harness → coordinates the entire system ✨ Agent → the resulting application-level behavior And this is where the interesting part begins: The Agent Harness is the key layer. A raw LLM can generate text and perform reasoning, but by itself it doesn't automatically know: - What tools it should use - When it should use them - What information it should retrieve - How to maintain state - How to execute multi-step tasks - How to interact with external systems - How to recover when something goes wrong The agent harness provides that missing orchestration layer. It can manage the loop: Understand → Plan → Retrieve → Act → Observe → Re-plan → Execute That is what turns a model from a powerful prediction engine into something that can behave like an agentic system. So the important distinction isn't necessarily: Computer vs. AI It is closer to: Traditional computing substrate → LLM-based computing substrate The architecture still has layers. The primitives have changed. And just like an operating system makes raw hardware useful to applications, an agent harness makes a raw LLM useful for complex, real-world tasks. 💡 The future of AI systems may depend as much on the orchestration layer around the model as on the model itself. Content: 🚨 Multi-Agent AI is powerful. But how do you debug an AI system when multiple agents, tools and LLM calls are working together? This is where AI Observability becomes critical. At Mindela, we’re exploring how technologies like Langfuse can make complex Agentic AI and Multi-Agent Systems easier to trace, evaluate and improve. Imagine a user asks: 💬 “Analyze customer churn and recommend what we should do next.” Behind that one request, an AI system might involve: 🧠 A Planner Agent breaking down the problem 🔎 A Retrieval Agent finding relevant information 🛠️ A Tool Agent querying APIs or databases 🎯 A Domain Agent interpreting the results ⚖️ An Evaluator checking response quality 🤖 An Orchestrator coordinating the entire workflow Now imagine trying to debug all of that without visibility. 👀 Langfuse helps add an observability layer across the AI workflow. You can understand traces across agents and tools, inspect prompts and responses, monitor latency and token usage, evaluate outputs, compare experiments and turn production traces into signals for improving the system. So instead of: ❌ Build → Deploy → Guess what went wrong AI teams can move toward: ✅ Build → Trace → Evaluate → Improve → Repeat That feedback loop becomes increasingly important as AI applications evolve from simple LLM calls into production-grade Agentic AI systems. At Mindela, we believe the future of AI engineering isn’t only about building smarter agents. Content: Limit Switches: How Machines Know When to Stop. One interesting component I'm learning about in Industrial Automation is the limit switch. A limit switch is an electromechanical device used to detect when a moving object or machine component reaches a predetermined position. In simple terms, it tells a control system: "The machine has reached this point." Limit switches can be used to: 🔹 Stop a motor when a mechanism reaches its end position. 🔹 Detect the position of moving machine parts. 🔹 Control conveyor systems. 🔹 Provide safety interlocking. 🔹 Trigger another operation in an automated process. A typical limit switch consists of a mechanical actuator and electrical contacts such as COM, NO (Normally Open), and NC (Normally Closed). What I find interesting is how a simple mechanical device can become an important part of an automated control system. I'm continuing to build my knowledge in TVET, Electrical Installation, and Industrial Automation, focusing not only on understanding components but also on how they work together in real-world systems. Question: Where have you seen a limit switch being used in a machine or automated system? Content: Your AWS bill has a line item nobody owns: data transfer. 💰 It isn't compute and it isn't storage, but on a multi-AZ EKS cluster it quietly climbs into the top of the invoice. ... Every byte a pod sends out through a NAT Gateway is metered at $0.045/GB on top of the hourly charge. ... Every call a service in one AZ makes to a replica in another crosses a zone boundary and gets billed in both directions. Nobody catches it because it never surfaces in the application. Latency looks fine, error rates look fine, and no dashboard has a row for it. It surfaces four weeks later, already spent, buried in a line item called "EC2-Other"... And most of it is topology, not volume: → One NAT Gateway per AZ instead of one shared across three → Gateway VPC endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB, which carry no hourly and no data processing charge at all → Load balancers in IP mode, so traffic stops taking an extra cross-zone hop through kube-proxy → 𝚝𝚛𝚊𝚏𝚏𝚒𝚌𝙳𝚒𝚜𝚝𝚛𝚒𝚋𝚞𝚝𝚒𝚘𝚗: 𝙿𝚛𝚎𝚏𝚎𝚛𝙲𝚕𝚘𝚜𝚎 on the "chatty" internal services in the Kubernetes cluster(s) ... We've run this cleanup on EKS clusters spread across multiple AZs & regions for our clients and do it almost daily. Nothing about the workload changed. The bytes just stopped taking the expensive route. If your cloud bill is growing faster than your traffic, that's usually a fixable pattern. We do this for SaaS and FinTech teams, and we're happy to take a look at yours. FinOps AWS Kubernetes CloudCost DevOps

Content: 🚨 Your EC2 instance crashed at 2 AM… but your users noticed NOTHING. How? That’s what a well-designed AWS High Availability architecture should achieve. Instead of depending on a single EC2 instance, production workloads can combine: ⚖️ Application Load Balancer (ALB) — distributes traffic across healthy instances ❤️ Health Checks — detect unhealthy targets and stop sending traffic to them 📈 Auto Scaling Group — maintains desired capacity and launches replacement instances 🌍 Multi-AZ Deployment — spreads workloads across Availability Zones to reduce single points of failure When an EC2 instance fails: EC2 Fails → Health Check Detects → ALB Redirects Traffic → Auto Scaling Replaces → Application Recovers ✅ 💡 Interview Tip: If asked how you'd design an EC2-based application for high availability, think beyond simply “add more servers.” Think: ALB + Health Checks + Auto Scaling + Multi-AZ 🔥 Production engineering isn't about assuming nothing will fail. Expect failure. Design for failure. Recover automatically. 📌 Save this post for your AWS interview preparation. AWS CloudComputing DevOps AWSArchitecture AWSInterview

Content: I thought Azure Databricks was just “Spark on Azure.” I was wrong. The more I learn about Databricks, the more I realize that Spark is only one piece of the puzzle. Here’s the mental model I’m building 👇 🔹 Azure Databricks = Lakehouse platform It brings together: → Data Engineering → SQL Analytics → Streaming → Machine Learning → Governance → BI All around the same data foundation. 🔹 The architecture finally started making sense Source → Ingest → ADLS → Bronze → Silver → Gold → SQL/BI/ML → Business Decisions And each layer has a purpose: 🟤 Bronze → Raw data ⚪ Silver → Cleaned & conformed data 🟡 Gold → Business-ready aggregates 🔹 Then comes Delta Lake This is where a data lake starts behaving more like a reliable database. Delta Lake provides: ✅ ACID transactions ✅ Schema enforcement & evolution ✅ Time travel ✅ MERGE / UPSERT ✅ UPDATE / DELETE ✅ Batch + streaming support A simple way to remember it: Delta Lake = Parquet + Transaction Log + Reliability 🔹 And Spark is the processing engine The concepts I’m focusing on: • Lazy evaluation • Transformations vs Actions • Narrow vs Wide transformations • Shuffles • Partitions • Driver & Executors • Catalyst optimization One concept that really clicked for me: Transformations build the plan. Actions execute the plan. 🔹 Then there’s the Azure side ADLS Gen2 → storage ADF → ingestion & orchestration Databricks → processing & analytics Unity Catalog → governance Power BI → visualization Instead of memorizing individual services, I’m trying to understand how they work together in a real pipeline. That shift in perspective has made learning Databricks much easier. I’m currently building my Azure Databricks notes from beginner → advanced, covering architecture, Spark, Delta Lake, ingestion, clusters, notebooks, SQL and more. For anyone learning Data Engineering: Don’t just learn the tools. Learn the data flow. Once the architecture makes sense, the tools start making sense too. Content: 📅 Dia 12 de 30 Desafio de Dados Databricks Professional ✨ Structured Streaming: Watermarks e Agregações com Estado Hoje entrei na parte mais temida da prova Professional: streaming com estado. Rodar agregações (como somas por janela de tempo) em um fluxo infinito de dados exige uma pergunta incômoda: até quando eu espero um dado atrasado antes de fechar a janela? 📎 O que aprendi hoje: Stateful Streaming: Operações como groupBy com janela de tempo mantêm um estado interno (guardado no checkpoint) que precisa ser limpo periodicamente, ou o cluster fica sem memória. Watermarks: É o mecanismo que define a tolerância a atraso. Um withWatermark("timestamp", "10 minutes") diz ao Spark: "aceite dados até 10 minutos atrasados; depois disso, descarte e libere o estado daquela janela". Trade-off: Watermark curto libera memória mais rápido, mas descarta dados legitimamente atrasados (ex: um evento de celular sem sinal). Watermark longo é mais tolerante, mas acumula estado e aumenta custo. Insight: A pegadinha clássica é achar que watermark filtra dados na entrada. Na verdade, ele só define quando o estado de uma janela pode ser descartado — dados atrasados além do limite são simplesmente ignorados na agregação, não geram erro. ✨ Reflexão Diária Streaming não é sobre processar rápido, é sobre decidir conscientemente o equilíbrio entre completude do dado e uso de memória. 💫💻📚🌸🎯 Dia: 02/04/2026 📌 Portfólio: ericaignatios.com.br 🌸 Blog: kirabyte.com.br 📸 Instagram: 🎥 Youtube: 💻 GitHub: github.com/ericaabrantes databricks estudos dados engenhariadedados structuredstreaming watermark sparkstreaming desafio30dias cozyengineer

Content: MERGE Delta Table ทำ SCD Type 2 ให้เร็วขึ้น ด้วยเทคนิค Hashing เคยไหม เขียน MERGE ทำ SCD Type 2 แล้วรันช้ามาก ยิ่ง column เยอะ ยิ่งรอนาน Delta Table คือ table format ที่รันอยู่บน Databricks รองรับ ACID transaction รองรับ UPDATE DELETE MERGE ได้เหมือนฐานข้อมูลทั่วไป พอมี MERGE เราเลยเอามาทำ SCD Type 2 ได้สะดวก เทียบ source กับ target คำสั่งเดียว เจอ key เดิมแต่ข้อมูลเปลี่ยน ก็ปิด record เก่า เจอ key ใหม่ ก็ insert เพิ่ม ไม่ต้องเขียน logic แยกเป็นหลาย step เหมือนเมื่อก่อน ปัญหาคือ ตอนเช็คว่า record เปลี่ยนไหม เรามักเทียบทีละ column col1 <> col1 OR col2 <> col2 OR col3 <> col3 ... พอ column เยอะ query ยาวจนอ่านไม่ไหว Spark ต้อง evaluate ทุก column ทุก row ช้าอย่างเห็นได้ชัด ทางแก้ที่เราใช้ คือ hashing รวม column ที่ track การเปลี่ยนแปลง hash ให้เหลือ column เดียว ชื่อ row_hash sha2(concat_ws("||", col1, col2, col3), 256) ตอน MERGE เทียบแค่ row_hash column เดียว ไม่ต้องเขียน OR ยาวเป็นสิบบรรทัดอีกต่อไป ผลลัพธ์คือ query plan เบาลง Spark เทียบแค่ 1 column แทนที่จะเทียบทีละสิบ column performance ต่างกันชัดเจน ข้อควรระวังนิดนึง column ที่มีค่า null ต้อง coalesce ก่อน hash ไม่งั้น hash จะไม่ตรงตามที่ควรจะเป็น เทคนิคเล็ก ๆ แบบนี้แหละ ที่ทำให้ pipeline ที่เคยรันเป็นชั่วโมง เหลือแค่ไม่กี่นาที ลองเอาไปปรับใช้กับงานของทุกคนดูนะ DataSparkTH Databricks DeltaLake DataEngineering

Content: Everyone's telling you to switch to Polars. Here's what they're not explaining. 🐼 → Pandas was built for 2008 hardware — few cores, small datasets, memory as the bottleneck. Polars was designed for the many-core, Rust-enabled world we're in now. → The syntax looks nearly identical. The speed gap isn't really about Rust — it's two architectural choices: parallel execution across cores, and lazy execution that optimizes your whole query before running it. → Memory matters as much as CPU: Polars' columnar Arrow format keeps analytical operations touching neighboring memory blocks instead of jumping around row by row. → Faster isn't automatically better. Pandas still wins for small datasets, notebooks, and teaching — the entire ML/viz ecosystem assumes it. Save this before your next "should I switch" debate 🔖 ⚠️ Worth flagging: this piece cites "different benchmarks" for the speed claims but never names a single figure or source — treat it as a conceptual primer, not proof you should migrate. Content: I started working with SQL around 2011. Two things always frustrated me: 1. No real modularity. I watched colleagues write 40,000–50,000 line files in Oracle. Everything stuffed into one massive script. Readability and maintenance were a nightmare. 2. Zero clear lineage. In large ETL pipelines (raw → silver → gold), it was almost impossible to answer: “Where did this table actually come from?” “Which upstream tables and transformations produced this final table?” Years later I discovered dbt. They combined SQL with Jinja templates. Suddenly you could: • Break logic into small, reusable models • Reference other models cleanly with ref() • Structure transformations properly • And most importantly — automatically see the full lineage of every table It felt like SQL++ with proper software engineering practices. Especially for ETL work, this combination of modularity + lineage is a game changer. That’s why I believe dbt Core stands out. This is what I know from my experience. If anyone has a better way to modularize SQL (or improve lineage visibility), please feel free to comment. Content: SEO alone is no longer enough. A few years ago, the customer journey looked like this: Google → Click → Website Today, it’s very different. People want answers immediately. Sometimes from a featured snippet. Sometimes from AI Overviews. Sometimes from ChatGPT, Gemini, or Perplexity. Sometimes through voice search. Search is no longer just about finding websites. It’s about finding the best answer. That’s why SEO alone isn’t enough anymore. Today, three disciplines work together: 🔍 SEO (Search Engine Optimization) Helps your content get discovered and rank in search results. 💬 AEO (Answer Engine Optimization) Helps your content become the direct answer to users’ questions. 🤖 GEO (Generative Engine Optimization) Helps AI systems understand, trust, and reference your content when generating responses. Think of it like this: 📈 SEO: “Help people find me.” 💡 AEO: “Show me as the answer.” 🚀 GEO: “Use me as a trusted source.” The biggest shift isn’t the algorithms. It’s how people search. They’re asking longer questions. Expecting instant answers. Comparing multiple sources before making a decision. That means modern content needs more than keywords. It needs: ✅ Clear structure ✅ Direct, answer-first content ✅ Real expertise ✅ Strong topical authority ✅ Semantic internal linking ✅ Trust signals ✅ Content that’s easy for both people and AI systems to understand If you’re still optimizing only for rankings, you’re only playing half the game. The future belongs to brands that can be: Found by search engines. Chosen by users. Referenced by AI. That’s what modern organic visibility looks like. Search has evolved. Your content strategy should too. 🚀 hashtagSEO hashtagAEO hashtagGEO hashtagAISearch hashtagContentStrategy hashtagDigitalMarketing

Content: **Influencer-Kooperationen klar vereinbaren** Heute aus der LEGAL-SMART-Praxis: Eine Fashion-E-Commerce-Marke plant langfristige Kooperationen mit mehreren Lifestyle-Influencern. Im Marketing steht die Kampagne bereits – offen ist jedoch, wer den produzierten Content wie lange, auf welchen Kanälen und für welche Werbeformate nutzen darf. Oft wird angenommen, dass mit der Bezahlung automatisch umfassende Nutzungsrechte übertragen sind. Auch Kennzeichnungspflichten, Exklusivität und die Verantwortung für rechtswidrige Inhalte bleiben in der Praxis nicht selten nur mündlich besprochen. Der juristische Wendepunkt: Veröffentlichung und Vergütung allein schaffen noch keine eindeutige Rechteverteilung. Verträge sollten deshalb Nutzungsumfang, Laufzeit, Bearbeitungsrechte, Freigabeprozesse und Konkurrenzkooperationen konkret regeln. Ebenso wichtig sind klare Zuständigkeiten für Werbekennzeichnung, Musik-, Bild- und Markenrechte sowie der Umgang mit möglichen Rechtsverstößen. Haftungsregelungen können Verantwortungsbereiche ordnen, beseitigen aber nicht automatisch Ansprüche Dritter. So wird aus einer spontanen Zusammenarbeit ein nachvollziehbarer Prozess. **Vorher: offene Erwartungen und Unsicherheit. Nachher: klare Rechte, Zuständigkeiten und planbare Abläufe.** Wer Influencer-Kooperationen vorbereitet, sollte Verträge und Compliance-Prozesse frühzeitig prüfen lassen. Content: Medical technology startup Ayati Devices has secured ₹15 crore ($1.5 million) in pre-Series A funding in a round led by Inflexor Ventures. Founded in 2019 by Nishant Kathpal, the Bengaluru-based company focuses on diagnostic technologies for diabetic foot complications and peripheral vascular disease. The company plans to deploy the new capital towards commercialisation, strengthening its manufacturing capabilities, expanding its domestic and international footprint, and increasing investments in research and artificial intelligence. Its portfolio includes Vibrasense, Vibrasense+T, Vasosense, Angiocam and the PODIA Trolley, covering assessments across neuropathy, blood flow, microcirculation and plantar pressure. Ayati Devices says its platform has been deployed across 30 countries, with more than 10,000 devices deployed and over 1 million screenings enabled. Content: 📅 Dia 13 de 30 Desafio de Dados Databricks Professional ✨ Triggers, Checkpoints e o Mito do Exactly-Once Hoje aprofundei como o Structured Streaming garante (ou tenta garantir) que cada registro seja processado exatamente uma vez, mesmo quando o cluster cai no meio de um processamento. 📎 O que aprendi hoje: Checkpoints: A cada micro-batch processado, o Spark grava no checkpoint location o progresso exato (quais offsets já foram lidos da fonte e já foram gravados no destino). Se o job cair, ele retoma exatamente de onde parou. Trigger Modes: ProcessingTime roda em intervalos fixos; AvailableNow processa tudo que existe hoje e desliga sozinho (ótimo pra economizar cluster em jobs incrementais); Continuous processa com latência ultrabaixa, mas com garantias mais fracas. Idempotência: "Exactly-once" no Spark é, na prática, "at-least-once no processamento + idempotência na escrita". O Delta Lake garante isso via transações ACID: se o mesmo micro-batch for reprocessado, o commit duplicado é identificado e ignorado. Insight: é importante testar cenários de mudança de código no meio do streaming: se você alterar a lógica de transformação e reiniciar o job com o mesmo checkpoint, o comportamento pode ser imprevisível — a boa prática é sempre avaliar se a mudança exige um novo checkpoint do zero. ✨ Reflexão Diária Confiar cegamente no "exactly-once" sem entender o papel do checkpoint é o tipo de armadilha que só aparece em produção, na pior hora possível. 💫💻📚🌸🎯 Dia: 03/04/2026 📌 Portfólio: ericaignatios.com.br 🌸 Blog: kirabyte.com.br 📸 Instagram: 🎥 Youtube: 💻 GitHub: github.com/ericaabrantes databricks estudos dados engenhariadedados structuredstreaming checkpoints idempotencia desafio30dias cozyengineer

Content: Databricks ran 4 coding-agent harnesses on its own multi-million-line codebase, and the same AI model cost 2.08X more depending on which one it used. Same model. Same thinking effort. The only thing that changed was the harness, and Databricks tested four different model-and-effort pairs to check it wasn't one lucky setting. Every time, the minimal harness Pi came out cheaper: 2.08X on Opus 4.8 at high effort, 1.46X at xhigh effort (with a 2-point higher pass rate), and 1.44X on GPT-5.5 at xhigh effort. The gap traces back to context. On Opus 4.8, Claude Code sent 742K tokens per task. Pi sent 236K, a gap of 3.2X, finishing tasks in fewer runs with a tighter working set. Quality wasn't identical across the board. Pi's pass rate ranged from 7 points below the bigger harness to 2 points above it. The cost gap held in all four pairs regardless, and that's the part most teams aren't pricing in. Sources: Databricks, "Benchmarking Coding Agents on Databricks' Multi-Million Line Codebase," 08 Jul 2026, databricks.com/blog AI Databricks Benchmark CodingAgents DevTools

Content: Hadoop Federation Explained: Scaling Distributed Storage Beyond a Single Namespace As data volumes continue to grow, a traditional single-NameNode HDFS architecture can face scalability and metadata management challenges. This is where Hadoop Federation becomes important. In our latest blog, we explore how Hadoop Federation enables organizations to scale distributed storage by introducing multiple independent namespaces, each managed by its own NameNode. Key topics covered include: Multiple Namespaces: Distribute metadata management across multiple NameNodes instead of relying on a single namespace. Improved Scalability: Reduce metadata bottlenecks and support massive storage environments. Better Resource Utilization: Distribute workloads across NameNodes according to organizational and application requirements. Enhanced Security: Apply namespace-specific access controls and security policies for different data domains. Load Balancing: Strategically distribute namespaces and workloads to prevent individual NameNodes from becoming bottlenecks. Fault Tolerance: Combine federation with appropriate failover and high-availability strategies to improve resilience. Monitoring & Performance Tuning: Continuously monitor NameNode performance and optimize the federation as data volumes evolve. Hadoop Federation demonstrates an important principle in distributed systems: scaling isn't always about making one component bigger, it can also mean distributing responsibility across multiple components. For organizations managing massive Hadoop environments, federation can provide a more flexible architecture for scaling storage, metadata management, and workloads. Content: Databases change. Managing those changes matters. Migration practices that work: 📋 Version controlled migrations - track every change 🔄 Idempotent scripts - safe to run multiple times ⬆️ Forward only - avoid down migrations in production 🧪 Test migrations against production-like data 🚀 Run migrations before deploying code Tools that help: Flyway, Liquibase, Alembic, Rails migrations. Pick one that fits your stack. Large table migrations need care. Online DDL, shadow tables, gradual rollouts. Locking production tables is not acceptable. Separate schema changes from data changes. Different risks, different timing. Never modify a deployed migration. Create a new one instead. Database changes deserve as much rigor as code changes. What's your migration strategy? Content: AI agents are getting smarter about when to stop you. Recently, we saw two big changes that matter in real life: First, **classifier-based safety gates**. Instead of asking permission for every step, the agent only interrupts for high-risk actions. Second, **auto-continue agents**. If the agent hits a usage limit, it can pause and then resume when limits reset, so you do not have to re-prompt everything. Why this is a win: less busywork, less “start over,” and safer pacing of actions. If you try an agent tool, here are 3 quick questions: 1) Does it interrupt me too much for low-risk work? 2) Does it ask at the right moment for risky actions? 3) When it resumes, does it keep the same plan? The real future of AI agents is not just “more tasks.” It is smoother workflows that still protect people at the risky points. Content: Here's a quick test for whether your data platform is actually working. Count how many new reports your team built last quarter. Then count how many decisions changed. Most mid-market data stacks I look at are technically fine. Snowflake is running. Power BI is connected. Refreshes are green. And every new question from leadership still produces one more report, built by the single analyst who knows which tables are the good ones. That is not a BI problem. It's a modeling problem wearing a BI costume. When the model underneath doesn't carry the business definitions, the visualization layer becomes the place people patch them in, one report at a time. The tell is easy to spot. If two dashboards disagree and the fix is a meeting rather than a query, your definitions live in people instead of in the model. Fix the model and the reports stop multiplying on their own. At SourceMash, we start at the model, not the dashboard. Content: Databricks has acquired Electric, a company building data infrastructure for AI agents, bringing its lightweight Postgres database and real-time synchronization technology into Databricks' platform. Electric's PGlite allows individual AI agents to run their own local Postgres database inside an application or agent sandbox, giving them fast access to the data and context they need while operating. Electric's synchronization engine can then keep distributed agent state aligned with a central Lakebase database, allowing multiple agents to work with shared information without constantly depending on a remote database. Databricks says the acquisition extends its Postgres capabilities from the data lakehouse toward the environments where AI agents actually execute. The move highlights an emerging infrastructure requirement for agentic AI: agents need their own local, persistent data and state, while still being able to coordinate with other agents and centralized systems. As AI applications become more autonomous and data-intensive, the database layer underneath those agents is becoming an increasingly important part of the technology stack. Content: 😏【現代的 CAD不只比「畫得快」 ─ Onshape 讓您的資料一路跟著產品走才是王道】 一個真正複雜的產品，從來不只是一個 3D Model。它可能同時牽涉到機構設計、PCB、Simulation、製造、檢驗，甚至是 Robotics 與 AI。 問題也因此開始出現： 🤔 當資料從 ECAD 交到 MCAD，會不會變成另一份檔案？ 🤔 當設計進入 Simulation，分析結果是不是又成為另一個孤立的資料？ 🤔 當工程師修改尺寸或公差，製造與品保端能不能立即看到正確的資訊？ 很多企業的 CAD 流程，真正耗費時間的地方，往往不是「設計」本身，而是這些資料在不同工具、不同部門與不同版本之間不斷被傳遞、轉換與重新確認。 而這正是 Onshape 最新產品發展所要解決的問題。 🤲 Connected Product Development——讓產品資料保持連續。 最新版本進一步強化了 Onshape 與 Altium 365 的 cloud-to-cloud ECAD/MCAD 協作。PCB 資料可以直接進入 Onshape PCB Studio，機構工程師可以在產品的 3D 環境中檢查板件、連接器、外殼與安裝空間，而不必依賴傳統的檔案匯出、轉換與來回傳遞。 🫡 這代表什麼？ 工程師不需要再一直問：「你現在用的是哪一版？」、「PCB 檔案更新了嗎？」、「這個零件是不是最新版本？」、「我收到的到底是哪一份資料？」 因為 Onshape 的核心思維，本來就不是把 CAD 當成一堆散落在電腦裡的檔案，而是讓設計資料成為一個持續存在、持續更新、持續被團隊使用的環境。 👉 而這個概念，也延伸到了 Simulation。 最新功能讓 Simulation Results 可以直接持續儲存在 Cloud 中，即使工程師關閉瀏覽器、關閉電腦，分析結果仍然保留在文件裡，團隊可以在不同裝置上查看，也可以直接比較不同 Load Case 與設計迭代。 對研發團隊而言，這個改變其實非常重要。因為 Simulation 的價值從來不只是「算出一個結果」。真正重要的是：「這個結果，能不能與設計演變的過程一起被保存、比較與理解？」 🤔 再看看 MBD。 Onshape 將 Model Based Definition 直接融入平台，工程師可以針對尺寸、公差、幾何公差等 Annotation 進行篩選，甚至直接在 Annotation 上留下 Comments 與 Action Items，並與模型及 Inspection Table 互相連結。 這讓設計、製造與品質之間的溝通，不再只是「看圖說話」。 而是讓設計意圖本身成為可以被追蹤、討論與傳遞的資料。 對 Robotics 開發而言，Onshape 最新的 URDF Export 也進一步支援 OBJ、STL、GLTF 等 Mesh 格式與解析度控制，並改善 Assembly 運動過程中的量測與 Clearance Checking，讓 CAD 與後續的 Robotics Simulation 環境之間更加連貫。 這些更新看似分散。 😣 ECAD 是一個功能。 😣 Simulation 是一個功能。 😣 MBD 是一個功能。 😣 Robotics 又是另一個功能。 但把它們放在一起看，就會發現 Onshape 真正想建立的並不是「功能越來越多的 CAD」。 而是一個不同工程工作可以共同使用的Cloud-Native Product Development Platform。 更值得注意的是，Onshape 的產品更新採取約每三週一次的自動發布週期，新的功能、改善與修正會直接進入平台，不需要傳統桌面軟體常見的下載、Patch、版本升級或 IT 部署流程。 這就是 Onshape 與傳統 File-Based CAD 思維最大的不同之一： 🙅‍♂️ 「傳統 CAD 管理的是檔案。」 🙆‍♂️ 「Onshape 管理的是產品資料與產品開發流程。」 當企業開始面對跨部門協作、遠端研發、供應鏈協同、電子與機構整合，以及越來越多 Simulation、Robotics 與 AI 工作流程時，CAD 的價值也正在重新定義。 未來真正具有競爭力的工程平台，不只是讓工程師把產品「畫出來」。而是讓產品從 Concept、Design、Simulation，一直到 Manufacturing 與 Inspection 的資料，都能夠持續連得起來。 這正是 Onshape 最新發展所呈現出的方向。 設計不應該只是產生一個檔案。 設計，應該成為一條持續連結產品生命週期的資料鏈。 聯絡我們｜桂源科技股份有限公司 電話｜(02) 2796-8933｜(04) 2700-3289 Onshape CloudCAD CloudNativeCAD CAD PDM ECAD MCAD Simulation MBD Robotics Content: 🧠 Reserved Concurrency vs Event Source Maximum Concurrency Both control Lambda concurrency — but they control different things. 👀 🛡️ Reserved Concurrency Controls the total concurrency of a Lambda function. 🚦 Event Source Maximum Concurrency Controls how much concurrency one SQS queue can use to invoke that Lambda. Think of it like this: 🛡️ Reserved = Function-level limit 🚦 Event Source Max = Queue-level limit Example Lambda Function → Reserved = 500 Queue A → Max = 100 Queue B → Max = 200 So Queue A can't consume more than 100, and Queue B can't consume more than 200. Together, they can use up to 300, while the function itself can use up to 500. 💡 Key idea: Use Event Source Maximum Concurrency to control traffic from individual SQS queues. Use Reserved Concurrency to control the total concurrency of the Lambda function. Together, they help prevent one busy queue from consuming all available capacity. 🚀 💬 Which one would you use to protect a Lambda function from one noisy SQS queue? Content: Refactored a working AWS setup into Terraform modules and hit a race condition doing it. Took my VPC + bastion + private app server + load balancer project and restructured it: pulled the networking (VPC, subnets, NAT gateway, routing) into a reusable module, with the rest of the project calling it instead of defining everything flat in one place. The refactor itself was straightforward, move the code, update every reference to go through the module's outputs instead of the resources directly. Missed a couple of references on the first pass and got clear "undeclared resource" errors pointing me right to them. The real issue showed up after a full rebuild: the app server booted and tried to install its web server before the NAT Gateway had actually finished becoming available. No error, no crash, the instance just quietly had no internet access yet, so the install failed silently in the background. Everything looked fine until I checked the load balancer's health check and saw it wasn't passing. Traced it back through the boot logs, confirmed the NAT Gateway needed more time than the instance did to come online, then rebuilt just the app server once the network was actually ready. Same infrastructure, same security posture now organized as something reusable instead of a one-off script. AWS Terraform InfrastructureAsCode CloudEngineering DevOps modules

Content: Databricks set out to raise $1 billion. Investors offered $15 billion. It took $5 billion, at a $190 billion valuation, and walked away from the other ten. The context that makes the decision rational: roughly $7 billion of revenue run rate, growing 80%, and already cash flow positive. A company in that position does not need the money. Taking it would just mean owning less. Which inverts the thing founders are taught. Raising the largest round available used to be the win. Here the flex is refusing it. Capital stopped being the scarce input in this market a while ago. Allocation is what is scarce now, and the companies with pricing power are the ones choosing how little to accept. Content: Databricks has closed a $5 billion funding round at a $190 billion valuation, according to TechCrunch, in what is already one of the most talked-about private fundraises of 2026. The original plan was modest by Silicon Valley standards — raise $1 billion, keep things tidy. But when the round opened, investor demand ballooned to an extraordinary $15 billion. CEO Ali Ghodsi ultimately settled on $5 billion, effectively turning away $10 billion in capital that investors were actively trying to hand him. Ghodsi's reasoning, as shared with TechCrunch, was direct: "AI is expensive." The implication being that even $5 billion may not be the last time Databricks comes back to the market. Worth noting: There's something quietly remarkable about a company negotiating *down* from a flood of investor money. It flips the usual startup narrative on its head — instead of founders chasing capital, capital is chasing founders. That kind of leverage signals how intensely the market is betting on AI infrastructure as the backbone of the next decade, not just the apps built on top of it. At a $190 billion valuation, Databricks now sits comfortably among the most valuable private companies on the planet — a number that would have seemed absurd for a data and AI platform just a few years ago. Does a $190B private valuation feel grounded in real fundamentals to you — or are we watching AI hype inflate another bubble? 👇 Source: TechCrunch ➡️

Content: 📊 Handling Missing Data in Large-Scale Scraping Projects Large-scale scraping projects often collect thousands of records from multiple sources, but missing fields can affect data quality, analytics, and business decisions. A structured approach to missing data handling helps businesses identify data gaps, recover valuable information, validate records, and maintain reliable datasets throughout recurring scraping workflows. Key Benefits of Handling Missing Data: ✔️ Monitor field-level data completeness ✔️ Identify recurring extraction gaps ✔️ Detect temporary scraping failures ✔️ Validate selectors after website changes ✔️ Recover missing information through retries and alternate sources ✔️ Cross-check important attributes across datasets ✔️ Maintain data quality throughout processing pipelines ✔️ Create cleaner and more reliable analytics datasets Effective missing data management goes beyond simply deleting incomplete records. Businesses can evaluate why information is missing, determine whether it can be recovered, and apply controlled validation or exclusion rules. By combining automated validation, recovery processes, historical comparisons, and cross-source verification, organizations can improve the reliability of large-scale scraped datasets. Content: 🚀 **DAY 10 OF 30 — REAL-TIME + STREAMING DATA PLATFORMS** Your competitor detected fraud in **12 milliseconds.** Your system found it **4 hours later** — in a batch report. That’s the difference between **Batch vs Streaming.** ⚡ ━━━━━━ 📦 **BATCH PROCESSING — THE OLD WAY** ━━━━━━ Collect Data → Wait → Process → Act ❌ Fraud detected too late ❌ Customers may already leave ❌ Opportunities disappear ❌ Dashboards show stale insights Batch processing still works for things like payroll and scheduled reports — but not when decisions need to happen **now.** ━━━━━━ ⚡ **STREAM PROCESSING — THE NEW STANDARD** ━━━━━━ Events Flow → Process Instantly → Act Immediately Every event is processed as it arrives. ✅ Real-time fraud detection ✅ Live recommendations ✅ Instant anomaly detection ✅ Real-time supply-chain tracking **No waiting. No stale data.** ━━━━━━━━━━━━ 🔧 **MODERN STREAMING PIPELINE** ━━━━━━━━━━━━ **DATA SOURCES → MESSAGE BROKER → STREAM PROCESSOR → STORAGE → ACTION** 📍 Sources — IoT, clicks, logs, APIs 📍 Broker — Kafka, Pulsar, AWS Kinesis 📍 Processor — Flink, Spark Streaming 📍 Storage — Redis, Cassandra, TimescaleDB 📍 Action — Dashboards, AI decisions, alerts The goal? **Turn data into action in milliseconds.** ━━━━━━━━━━━━ 🌍 **4 INDUSTRIES USING REAL-TIME DATA** ━━━━━━━━━━━━ 🔹 **Finance** — Detect suspicious transactions instantly 🔹 **E-commerce** — Personalise experiences while users browse 🔹 **DevOps** — Detect infrastructure issues before downtime 🔹 **Logistics** — Track shipments live across the supply chain ━━━━━━━━━━━━ 💡 **3 KEY TAKEAWAYS** ━━━━━━━━━━━━ 🔹 Batch creates **lag** — lag creates risk 🔹 Streaming enables decisions **at the moment they matter** 🔹 Kafka, Flink & Kinesis power modern real-time platforms **The future belongs to businesses that act in milliseconds — not hours.** 👇 **Tell me:** Is your business using **Batch or Real-Time Streaming?** What’s the biggest challenge you’ve faced with real-time data? 🔔 Follow for **Day 11 — Self-Optimising Databases** RealTimeData StreamProcessing ApacheKafka DataEngineering Flink DataPlatform MLOps CloudNative SarmakSolution 30DayChallenge FutureOfTech

Content: We built ChiselForge, an open-source web extraction engine for turning web pages into structured data without writing a custom scraper for every website. The idea was simple: start with the most reliable signal available and only escalate when necessary. ChiselForge follows a deterministic-first extraction pipeline: → Structured data such as JSON-LD and other structured sources → Embedded application and hydration data → Page content → Browser rendering for dynamic websites → AI-assisted extraction when deterministic methods aren't enough It also goes beyond single-page extraction with web crawling, sitemap discovery, link discovery, concurrent extraction, browser automation and pause/resume workflows. We built it because we needed a better way to handle web scraping, structured data extraction and large-scale data pipelines. Now we're making it open source. GitHub: If you're working with web scraping, web crawling, data engineering, AI agents, browser automation, structured data or AI workflows, ChiselForge is worth a look. Content: Dados não se teleportam. 😌 Quando uma informação precisa sair de um sistema e chegar a outro lugar, existe um caminho entre esses dois pontos. Nesse caminho, os dados podem ser movidos, organizados, transformados, validados, armazenados... E esse fluxo organizado tem um nome: pipeline de dados. Uma forma simples de guardar a ideia é: origem → etapas → destino Não significa que todo pipeline tenha exatamente as mesmas etapas — ou que todo pipeline seja um ETL. ETL pode fazer parte desse caminho. O pipeline representa o fluxo mais amplo. Transformar → ETL Transportar → Pipeline Coordenar → 👀 Se “pipeline” parecia uma palavra muito mais complicada antes deste post, salva esta imagem mental para não esquecer. Content: Ab wann reicht dein Eigenkapital? Der häufigste Grund, mit dem Kauf zu warten: „Mein Eigenkapital reicht noch nicht — sonst wären die Zinsen zu hoch.“ Es reicht meistens früher, als gedacht. Denn mehr Eigenkapital heißt nicht automatisch mehr Rendite. Zwei Käufer, dieselbe Wohnung für 250.000 €. In 15 Jahren steigt sie um rund 62.500 € — für beide gleich, egal wer wie viel angezahlt hat. A hat 25.000 € eingesetzt. Der Gewinn entspricht dem 2,5-Fachen seines Einsatzes. B hat 200.000 € eingesetzt. Der Gewinn entspricht nicht einmal einem Drittel davon. Dir gehört der Wertzuwachs der ganzen Wohnung, auch wenn du nur einen Bruchteil bezahlt hast. Das ist der Hebel. Das Minimum sind deshalb die Kaufnebenkosten — rund 10 % vom Kaufpreis für Grunderwerbsteuer, Notar, Grundbuch und Makler. Die finanziert dir in der Regel keine Bank, den Kaufpreis sehr wohl. Aber damit ist die Frage noch nicht beantwortet. Wer nur die Nebenkosten deckt, finanziert den Kaufpreis voll — und zahlt genau deshalb den höchsten Zinssatz. Ab hier ziehen zwei Kräfte gegeneinander: Mehr Kredit hebelt deine Rendite nach oben. Der höhere Zins zieht sie wieder runter. Welche gewinnt, hängt an deinem Objekt und an den Beleihungsstufen deiner Bank. Eine allgemeingültige Zahl gibt es hier nicht — nur eine Rechnung. Kennst du jemanden, der gerade auf Eigenkapital spart? Schick ihm diesen Beitrag — er spart vielleicht auf eine Zahl, die er gar nicht braucht. Content: Insert a human review step only when an agent's error costs more than the delay of asking for one. That is the actual rule, not "add a human wherever it feels risky." Review has a price: latency, an interrupted workflow, someone's attention pulled away from other work. Skip that step on a low-stakes task and the system does not get less safe. It gets faster. Most teams place review by instinct. A refund request gets flagged because refunds sound sensitive, while a mislabeled support ticket routes on autopilot because misrouting looks minor. Neither call ran the actual math: what does the error cost if it ships, against what the pause costs if it does not. High-volume, cheap-to-fix mistakes do not need a human in the loop. A wrong classification that a downstream check catches, or an action that is trivial to undo, can run unattended. Save review for the decisions where being wrong is expensive and being slow is cheap by comparison. Over-indexing on safety has a cost too. It kills throughput and turns a workable agent into one nobody wants to run at scale. Link in bio. AIAgents AIEngineering LLMOps HumanInTheLoop ProductionAI

Content: An LLM can generate text. But give it tools, and something much more interesting happens. It can start interacting with external systems. For example, an AI agent could potentially: → Search the web → Query a database → Call an API → Execute code → Read files → Perform calculations → Take actions in software The basic difference is: LLM: Input → Generate → Output Agent: Observe → Reason → Choose Tool → Act → Observe Result → Repeat That feedback loop is what makes agentic systems so powerful. But it also creates a new engineering challenge. Once an AI can ACT, mistakes become more consequential. That's why real agentic systems need things like: → Guardrails → Permissions → Observability → Error handling → Human oversight So I don't think the interesting question is: “Can an LLM reason?” It's: “What can we safely allow it to do with that reasoning?” That's where agentic AI starts becoming a serious engineering problem. Would you trust an AI agent to take actions on your behalf without asking for confirmation? AI ArtificialIntelligence AIAgents AgenticAI LLM AIEngineering

Content: The rent versus own argument in cloud has been over for years. Everyone already rents. Nobody stops to ask which kind of renting the workload actually needs. A hyperscaler earns its markup in specific ways. A managed service catalog that saves you a build year, global regions that cut latency, and a durability option you can turn on if you pay for it. Compliance is the one people get wrong most often. Running on a certified provider inherits the infrastructure layer of the audit, not your application's certification. None of that means default to the biggest name every time. A plain stack of containers, Postgres, and object storage is often cheaper on an independent host once egress fees start eating a bootstrapped budget. Heavy GPU training frequently costs less on a neocloud too. Save this before your next architecture review. Which reason actually drives your cloud choice: the catalog, the compliance shortcut, the reach, or plain cost. Say it in the comments. Content: Databricks Just Raised $5B at a $190B Valuation Databricks wanted to raise a billion dollars. Investors wanted to hand them fifteen billion. They landed in the middle and closed a $5 billion round that puts the company at a $190 billion valuation. Half a year ago Databricks was valued at $134 billion. That’s a jump of $56 billion in roughly six months, and it happened while the company was already profitable enough not to need the cash that badly. Investors weren’t rescuing anything here. They were fighting to get a seat at the table. That kind of jump would raise eyebrows in most industries, but right now it barely registers as unusual. CEO Ali Ghodsi says the demand is coming from a very specific place, companies that are actually deploying AI agents now, not just testing them, and running headfirst into the cost of running all that inference at scale. Databricks sells the tools that help a business keep that spending under control, plus a database built specifically for AI agents called Lakebase, which has already crossed $100 million in yearly revenue on its own. The bigger number underneath all of this is Databricks’ total revenue run rate, which just crossed $7 billion, up more than 80 percent from a year ago. That is not hype money chasing a story. That is a company selling something enterprises are actually paying for every single month. What strikes me about this round is who’s in it. Blackstone, Goldman Sachs, T. Rowe Price, the kind of investors who do not throw money at things just because they’re trendy. When that crowd shows up for an AI infrastructure company at this size, it tells you enterprise AI spending is not slowing down anytime soon. Content: Databricks Asked For $1B. Investors Brought $15B. They raised $5B at a $190B valuation. $7B ARR. 80% growth year over year. Cash flow positive. Still private by choice. The entire industry spent the last 18 months benchmarking models. The smart money just wrote $15B of demand into the data layer that every model runs on. Databricks does not make a model. It makes the infrastructure that makes models useful at enterprise scale. That is a different business from the model race entirely. Three things this fundraise signals: 1. Enterprise data infrastructure is now priced as permanent infrastructure, not a venture bet. At $190B, this is valued like a utility. 2. Staying private when you are cash flow positive is the new power move. No dilutive IPO. No quarterly pressure. Just compound. 3. The benchmark race is a distraction from where the durable margin lives. Every AI product on every model still needs a data layer. That layer just repriced. When does a startup stop being a startup? When it pulls $15B of demand on a $1B ask and still does not need to go public. Content: Mesajlar doğru sırada gitmiyorsa suç Kafka'da değil, partition anahtarında. Çoğu ekip Kafka'yı 'garantili sıralı kuyruk' sanır. Oysa Kafka yalnızca aynı partition içinde sıralama garantisi verir. Anahtarı rastgele dağıtırsan, aynı kullanıcının 'sepete ekle' ve 'ödeme yap' event'leri farklı partition'lara düşer — tüketici tarafında ters sırada işlenir. Sonuç: ödeme, sipariş oluşmadan tetiklenir. Sessizce bozan üç nokta: 1) Partition key seçimi Sıralamanın korunması gereken birim neyse (userId, orderId, accountId) onu key yap. Böylece o varlığın tüm event'leri aynı partition'a, dolayısıyla aynı sıraya düşer. 2) Consumer'da paralellik tuzağı Bir partition'ı çok thread'le işlersen sırayı yine bozarsın. Sıra kritikse partition başına tek işleyici tut. 3) Retry sırayı ters çevirir Hatalı bir mesajı retry ederken sonraki mesaj çoktan işlenmiş olabilir. İdempotent tüketici + partition bazlı offset yönetimi şart. Özet: 'Kafka sıralamayı garanti eder' cümlesi eksik. Doğrusu: 'Kafka aynı partition içinde sıralamayı garanti eder.' Tasarımın bu cümlenin üzerine oturmalı. Dağıtık sistem mimarinizde sıralama, idempotency veya event tasarımı konuşmak isterseniz keşif görüşmesi ücretsiz. 👇 Sıralama sorununu üretimde yaşadın mı? Content: The SEO strategy of “one keyword, one page” is becoming too narrow. The bigger opportunity is topic ownership. Your brand should become strongly associated with the topics your customers care about across: • Google Search • AI search • Related queries • Commercial searches • Supporting content • Industry discussions I use this 4-step framework: 1. Define Choose the topics your brand needs to own. 2. Build Create connected content around the topic, its subtopics, entities, questions, and search intents. 3. Measure Track visibility across Google and AI search, then compare your topic coverage with competitors. 4. Expand Move into adjacent topics your audience cares about. The goal is not to rank for one keyword. The goal is to build enough depth and relevance for your brand to become strongly associated with an entire topic. That is where SEO, AEO, and GEO start working together. Topic ownership compounds when your content, internal links, authority, entities, and brand signals reinforce the same subject over time. Content: Honasa Consumer, which owns Mamaearth, recorded ₹756 crore in revenue from operations during Q1 FY27, compared with ₹595 crore a year earlier, marking 27% year-on-year growth. Profit after tax increased more than twofold to ₹90.45 crore from ₹41.33 crore in Q1 FY26. The company also reported ₹22.5 crore in non-operating income, taking overall revenue to ₹778 crore. EBITDA doubled to ₹110 crore during the quarter, resulting in an EBITDA margin of 14%. Honasa’s overall expenses rose to ₹659 crore from ₹564 crore. Material costs increased 34% to ₹229 crore, while employee benefit expenses rose 10% to ₹66 crore. The company said its recently acquired men’s grooming brand Reginald Men has grown more than 2X since the acquisition and now has an annual revenue run rate exceeding ₹150 crore. In June 2026, Honasa also acquired a 58% stake in nutraceuticals company Fluence Pharma at an enterprise value of around ₹135 crore. Operating revenue increased 15% sequentially from ₹657 crore in Q4 FY26, while profit rose 30.3% from ₹69.44 crore. Content: നാഷണൽ പേയ്‌മെന്റ് കോർപ്പറേഷൻ ഓഫ് ഇന്ത്യയുടെ (NPCI) കണക്കുകൾ പ്രകാരം ജൂലായ് മാസത്തിൽ നടന്ന യുപിഐ (UPI) ഇടപാടുകളിൽ 10.86 ബില്യൺ ഇടപാടുകളുമായി ഫോൺപേ (PhonePe) ഒന്നാം സ്ഥാനം നിലനിർത്തി. ഗൂഗിൾ പേ (Google Pay), പേടിഎം (Paytm) എന്നിവയാണ് യഥാക്രമം രണ്ടും മൂന്നും സ്ഥാനങ്ങളിൽ ഉള്ളത്. രാജ്യത്താകെ 29.88 ലക്ഷം കോടി രൂപ മൂല്യമുള്ള 23.66 ബില്യൺ യുപിഐ ഇടപാടുകളാണ് ഈ മാസം നടന്നത്; ഇതിൽ 86 ശതമാനത്തിലധികം ഇടപാടുകളും ഈ ആദ്യ മൂന്ന് ആപ്പുകൾ വഴിയാണ് നടന്നത്. നാവി (Navi), സൂപ്പർ.മണി (super.money), ഭീം (BHIM), ക്രെഡ് (CRED), വാട്സ്ആപ്പ് തുടങ്ങിയവയാണ് മറ്റ് പ്ലാറ്റ്‌ഫോമുകളെങ്കിലും, മൊത്തം യുപിഐ വിപണിയിൽ ഫോൺപേയുടെയും ഗൂഗിൾ പേയുടെയും വ്യക്തമായ ആധിപത്യമാണ് ഇപ്പോഴുമുള്ളത്. സൂര്യനിൽ ഊർജ്ജം ഉൽപ്പാദിപ്പിക്കുന്ന പ്രക്രിയയായ ന്യൂക്ലിയർ ഫ്യൂഷൻ (Nuclear Fusion) ഭൂമിയിലും അനുകരിച്ച് പരിധിയില്ലാത്ത ശുദ്ധമായ ഊർജ്ജം ഉൽപ്പാദിപ്പിക്കുക എന്ന മനുഷ്യൻ്റെ ലക്ഷ്യം അതിവേഗം യാഥാർത്ഥ്യത്തിലേക്ക് അടുത്തുകൊണ്ടിരിക്കുകയാണ്. ആർട്ടിഫിഷ്യൽ ഇന്റലിജൻസ്, കരുത്തുറ്റ കമ്പ്യൂട്ടർ ചിപ്പുകൾ, നൂതനമായ സൂപ്പർകണ്ടക്റ്റിംഗ് കാന്തങ്ങൾ എന്നിവയിലുണ്ടായ സാങ്കേതിക പുരോഗതിയും, ഈ മേഖലയിൽ അടുത്തിടെ നടന്ന വിജയകരമായ ശാസ്ത്രീയ പരീക്ഷണങ്ങളുമാണ് വൻകിട നിക്ഷേപകരെ ഇപ്പോൾ ഫ്യൂഷൻ സാങ്കേതികവിദ്യയിലേക്ക് ആകർഷിക്കുന്നത്. ഇതിന്റെ ഫലമായി കോമൺവെൽത്ത് ഫ്യൂഷൻ സിസ്റ്റംസ് (CFS), ഹീലിയോൺ (Helion), പസഫിക് ഫ്യൂഷൻ (Pacific Fusion) തുടങ്ങിയ നിരവധി പ്രൈവറ്റ് സ്റ്റാർട്ടപ്പുകൾ ഇതിനോടകം തന്നെ കോടിക്കണക്കിന് ഡോളറുകളുടെ നിക്ഷേപം സ്വന്തമാക്കിക്കഴിഞ്ഞു. ഓൺലൈൻ ട്രാവൽ അഗ്രിഗേറ്ററായ ഈസ്‌മൈട്രിപ്പിന് (EaseMyTrip) 2026-27 സാമ്പത്തിക വർഷത്തിലെ ഒന്നാം പാദത്തിൽ 11.7 കോടി രൂപയുടെ അറ്റനഷ്ടം നേരിട്ടു. മുൻ വർഷം ഇതേ കാലയളവിൽ 44 ലക്ഷം രൂപ ലാഭത്തിലായിരുന്ന കമ്പനിയുടെ മൊത്തം ചെലവുകൾ 29.8 ശതമാനം വർധിച്ച് 152.7 കോടി രൂപയിലെത്തിയതാണ് ഇപ്പോഴത്തെ നഷ്ടത്തിന് പ്രധാന കാരണമായത്. എന്നാൽ ഈ നഷ്ടത്തിനിടയിലും കമ്പനിയുടെ പ്രവർത്തന വരുമാനം 18.4 ശതമാനം ഉയർന്ന് 134.7 കോടി രൂപയായിട്ടുണ്ട്. വിമാന ടിക്കറ്റ്, ട്രെയിൻ, ബസ് ബുക്കിംഗുകളിൽ നിന്നുള്ള വരുമാനത്തിൽ ഇടിവുണ്ടായെങ്കിലും ഹോട്ടൽ പാക്കേജ് സേവനങ്ങളിൽ നിന്നുള്ള വരുമാനം ഇരട്ടിയായി വർധിച്ചതാണ് ഇതിന് സഹായിച്ചത്. entestartup startup startupindia startupbusiness startups startuptips startuplife

Content: WorldLink Communications is investing in Nepal’s digital infrastructure with the construction of a first-of-its-kind green data center in Matatirtha, Kathmandu, with support from IFC and the IDA Private Sector Window. Its subsidiary, Data World, is set to become Nepal’s largest data center operator with nearly 3 megawatts of capacity, while the facility will be the country’s first to receive EDGE green-building certification. WorldLink also plans up to 11 smaller EDGE-certified centers across the country, with construction already creating more than 1,000 jobs. The project aims to strengthen Nepal’s growing demand for data storage, cloud services and reliable digital connectivity. WorldLink currently serves more than 1.08 million households and businesses across 74 districts through a 15,000-kilometre fiber network. Once operational, the new data center is expected to create around 6,000 direct and indirect jobs, including 135 full-time positions in areas such as IT, cybersecurity, AI and cloud computing. With energy-efficient cooling, solar power and water-saving systems, the project is also designed to reduce environmental impact while supporting businesses, digital services and Nepal’s long-term economic growth. Content: ### AI Testing Notes 4: 5 Tests Every AI QA Engineer Should Run 🤖 Loops never stop by themselves. Check whether something makes them stop. When testing AI agents, apart from verifying that the final answer is correct, it is essential to test if the agent knows how and when to stop. The following 5 tests are crucial for any AI agent: 1️⃣ Step Limit Test: Does the agent stop when the number of steps is exceeded? 2️⃣ Tool Call Budget Test: Does the agent stop on calling the same tool multiple times? 3️⃣ Repeat Detection Test: Does the agent detect repeated actions? 4️⃣ Stop Condition Test: Does the agent stop when the objective is reached? 5️⃣ Context Growth Test: Does the agent prevent excessive growth of context and memory? The ultimate goal of an AI agent is not to provide the correct answer. The agent should be able to achieve the goal with minimal computational resources, time, and risk. 📒 AI Testing Notes - practical advice on building and testing AI agents. 👉 Follow SpurQLabs for more notes on testing AI agents, QA, and software testing in general! 🌐 aitesting aiagents agenticai softwaretesting engineeringmemes qualityassurance aiengineering llm testautomation qualityengineering qualityeducation softwarequality spurqlabs testingcommunity

ಜಾರ್ಜಿಯಾದ ಹುಂಡೈ ಪ್ಲಾಂಟ್‌ಗಳಲ್ಲಿ ರೋಬಾಟ್‌ಗಳು ಅತ್ಯಂತ ನಿಧಾನವಾಗಿ ಕೆಲಸ ಮಾಡುತ್ತಿರುವುದು ಬೆಳಕಿಗೆ ಬಂದಿದ್ದು, ಬಿಎಂಡಬ್ಲ್ಯೂ ಕಂಪನಿಯು ರೋಬಾಟ್‌ಗಳನ್ನು ಕೈಬಿಟ್ಟು 350 ನುರಿತ ಮ್ಯಾನುಫ್ಯಾಕ್ಚರಿಂಗ್ ಇಂಜಿನಿಯರ್‌ಗಳನ್ನು ನೇಮಿಸಿಕೊಂಡ ನಂತರ ಕಾರುಗಳ ಗುಣಮಟ್ಟ ಹಾಗೂ ಉತ್ಪಾದನಾ ವೇಗ ಗಣನೀಯವಾಗಿ ಹೆಚ್ಚಾಗಿದೆ. ಆಟೋಮೇಷನ್ ಕೊರತೆಯಿಂದ ಕೆಲಸ ನಿಧಾನವಾಗುತ್ತದೆ ಎಂಬ ಕಾರಣಕ್ಕೆ ಕಾರು ಕಂಪನಿಗಳು ರೋಬಾಟ್‌ಗಳನ್ನು ತಂದರೂ, ಅವು ಪದೇ ಪದೆ ತಾಂತ್ರಿಕ ದೋಷಕ್ಕೆ ಒಳಗಾಗಿ ಇಡೀ ಅಸೆಂಬ್ಲಿ ಲೈನ್ ಸ್ಥಗಿತಗೊಳ್ಳುವಂತೆ ಮಾಡುತ್ತಿದ್ದವು. ಟೆಸ್ಲಾ ಕಂಪನಿಯ ಎಲಾನ್ ಮಸ್ಕ್ ಕೂಡ ಈ ಹಿಂದೆ ಮಾದರಿ-3 ಕಾರುಗಳ ಉತ್ಪಾದನೆಯಲ್ಲಿ ಏಲಿಯನ್ ಡ್ರೆಡ್‌ನಾಟ್ ಎಂಬ ಸಂಪೂರ್ಣ ಮಾನವರಹಿತ ಸ್ವಯಂಚಾಲಿತ ಫ್ಯಾಕ್ಟರಿಯ ಕಲ್ಪನೆಯನ್ನು ಜಾರಿಗೆ ತರಲು ಹೋಗಿ ವಿಫಲರಾಗಿದ್ದರು. ವೈರಿಂಗ್ ಹಾಗೂ ಬ್ಯಾಟರಿ ಪ್ಯಾಕ್ ಜೋಡಣೆಯಲ್ಲಿ ರೋಬಾಟ್‌ಗಳ ವಿಫಲತೆಯನ್ನು ಒಪ್ಪಿಕೊಂಡಿದ್ದ ಮಸ್ಕ್, ಆಟೋಮೇಷನ್ ತಪ್ಪು, ಮನುಷ್ಯರ ಸಾಮರ್ಥ್ಯವನ್ನು ನಾವು ಕಡೆಗಣಿಸಿದ್ದೆವು ಎಂದು ಬಹಿರಂಗವಾಗಿ ಹೇಳಿದ್ದರು. ಅಂತೆಯೇ ಮರ್ಸಿಡೀಸ್-ಬೆಂಜ್ ಕಂಪನಿಯು ಸಹ ತನ್ನ ಜರ್ಮನಿಯ ಸಿಂಡೆಲ್‌ಫಿಂಗನ್ ಕಾರ್ಖಾನೆಯಲ್ಲಿ ಎಸ್-ಕ್ಲಾಸ್ ಕಾರುಗಳ ಉತ್ಪಾದನಾ ಸಾಲಿನಿಂದ ಬೃಹತ್ ರೋಬಾಟ್‌ಗಳನ್ನು ತೆಗೆದುಹಾಕಿ, ಗ್ರಾಹಕರ ವೈವಿಧ್ಯಮಯ ಆಯ್ಕೆಗಳಿಗೆ ತಕ್ಕಂತೆ ಬೇಗ ಸ್ಪಂದಿಸುವ ಮಾನವ Content: "Terraform state is easy to ignore, until it becomes your biggest problem." When I started learning Terraform, all my attention went to writing resources, VPCs, subnets, security groups, EC2 instances, and EKS clusters. That part feels satisfying because you can watch infrastructure appear in real time. Then I started understanding state. And I realised the .tf files are only half the story. Here's what Terraform state actually taught me, from working through AWS, Azure and GCP projects hands-on: State is Terraform's memory. It maps your configuration to the real resources running in your cloud account. Without it, Terraform can't determine what already exists, what needs updating, or what to destroy. It's not a side feature; it's fundamental to how Terraform works. Local state breaks down the moment infrastructure becomes a team effort. A terraform.tfstate file on your laptop means nobody else can safely run Terraform alongside you. The last person to run it wins, and everyone else's changes risk being overwritten. When I moved to an S3 backend with DynamoDB locking on my AWS projects, the reason for remote state with locking became immediately clear. One person runs terraform apply, the state locks, nobody else can run it simultaneously, the lock releases when it completes. No conflicts, no corruption. Drift is a real and quiet risk. When someone modifies a resource manually in the cloud console without updating the Terraform configuration, the state no longer reflects reality. The next terraform plan will try to revert those changes. This is why "if Terraform manages it, change it through Terraform" isn't just a preference; it's a state integrity discipline. State contains sensitive data. Database passwords, private keys, connection strings- if Terraform creates them, they live in state. Remote state needs encryption at rest and strict IAM access controls. This is something beginners often overlook until they realise what's actually inside that file. The biggest lesson: Infrastructure as Code isn't just about creating resources. It's about managing infrastructure safely, consistently and predictably, over time, across teams, with full auditability.

Content: Your MERGE operation can be slow even when the amount of changed data is small. Why? The answer often lies in how the data is physically organized. When CDC continuously updates a Delta table, an inefficient layout can cause MERGE to scan and rewrite more data than necessary. A better approach is to optimize the table for the way it is updated: 📦 Keep file sizes manageable 🔍 Organize data around frequently used MERGE columns ⚖️ Maintain sensible partition sizes ⚙️ Use automatic write optimization 🧹 Compact small files The goal is simple: Less data scanned + less data rewritten = faster MERGE operations. ⚡ This becomes increasingly important as the table grows and updates happen continuously. Think beyond the MERGE statement itself—the physical layout of your data can have a major impact on performance. Content: 🚀 Batch Processing vs Stream Processing — Every Data Engineer Should Know This! How should your data be processed — all at once or as it arrives? 📦 Batch Processing Collect data → Wait → Process together Best for scheduled jobs, historical analysis, ETL pipelines and periodic reporting. ⚡ Stream Processing Event arrives → Process immediately → Real-time result Best for fraud detection, live dashboards, IoT monitoring, clickstreams and real-time alerts. 💡 Easy way to remember: BATCH = WAIT → PROCESS STREAM = ARRIVE → PROCESS In real-world Data Engineering, it’s not about choosing one forever. A good architecture often uses both, depending on latency, volume and business requirements. 📌 Save this for your Data Engineering learning and interview preparation! Content: Dica avançada de AWS Athena: LAG() com ordenação determinística Você usa LAG() no AWS Athena para comparar um evento com o anterior? Então atenção a um detalhe que pode mudar o resultado: o timestamp sozinho nem sempre define uma ordem única. Se dois eventos do mesmo cliente têm o mesmo evento_ts, a linha anterior pode ficar ambígua. A solução é adicionar uma chave de desempate no ORDER BY, como evento_id. Exemplo: LAG(valor) OVER ( PARTITION BY cliente_id ORDER BY evento_ts, evento_id ) AS valor_anterior A lógica é simples, mas poderosa: PARTITION BY cliente_id define o grupo independente de cada cliente. ORDER BY evento_ts, evento_id define a sequência dos eventos. O evento_id funciona como desempate determinístico quando os timestamps coincidem. LAG(valor) recupera o valor da linha anterior dentro dessa sequência, permitindo calcular variações absolutas e percentuais. Outro cuidado: funções de janela podem consumir bastante memória em janelas muito grandes. Sempre que possível, filtre as partições do Athena e reduza o volume de dados antes de aplicar a janela. Dica prática: não pergunte apenas “qual é a linha anterior?”. Defina primeiro em qual grupo e segundo qual ordem. Você já encontrou resultados inconsistentes por causa de timestamps iguais? Content: Influencer Marketing - What Makes An Influencer Commercially Valuable An influencer is commercially valuable when they have a high engagement rate. This is shown by the number of likes, comments, shares and saves. An influencer can have a lot of followers but less engagement, this indicates running a campaign with them is less likely going to be a success. In contrast an influencer can have less followers but high engagement, this indicates that running a campaign with them is going to be a success. Another thing that makes an influencer commercially valuable is when their followers see them as a leader in their niche. People take advice and recommendations from people they see as expert in their fields, this increase trust and credibility. An influencer who is seen in the highest regard in their niche will likely sell more products or services as their followers will trust their recommendations. An influencer who produces high-quality content is commercially valuable because the brand can save costs and re-use their content on other platforms. This means their content meet the standards of being used on other platforms, saving the brand time and money to produce more content. Lastly what makes an influencer commercially valuable is the ability to track ROI through click throughs, usage of promo codes, affiliate links and direct sales data. influencermarketing commerciallyvaluable Featured Influencer:

Content: A 27B local workhorse now fits on a single 16GB consumer GPU. That is the real Qwen3.8-27B story. Released on August 14, Qwen3.8-27B is a dense multimodal model with a 262K native context window, support for extension up to 1M tokens, MTP speculative decoding, adjustable reasoning effort and an Apache 2.0 license. Qwen's own scorecard is striking: 73.0 on Terminal-Bench 2.1, 61.7 on SWE-bench Pro, 84.3 on OSWorld Verified and 89.2 on GPQA. Those numbers are company-reported, however. Evaluation harnesses differ, and some tests were run in-house. The early field reports may matter even more. One builder ran a custom IQ4_XS quant on an RTX 5060 Ti with 16GB of VRAM, a 32K context window and MTP-2 at roughly 47.5 tokens per second. Another used a 24GB RTX 3090 with a Q4_K_XL quant and 110K context to generate an e-commerce UI in roughly 20–30 minutes. Korean users reported the same split. A 16GB Q3 setup completed an inventory app at around 22–24 tokens per second, but showed looping and overthinking. A separate 50GB+ BF16 self-test placed Qwen only one point behind GPT-5.4—but that was a personal test, not an independent benchmark. And the failures were real. One Reddit agent run spent 28 hours before writing files, then moved from 71 compile errors to 84. Another user found the model four to five times slower than Qwen3.6-27B in OpenCode. That is not a contradiction. Hardware, quantization, context length, MTP settings and the task harness can change the model you actually experience. Florer's take: Qwen3.8-27B looks ready for bounded local work—private code, documents and repeatable tasks. It does not yet justify blind trust in long autonomous runs or high-cost-of-failure workflows. Fitting the model was the milestone. Trusting the workflow is the next one. Sources: Qwen GitHub and model card; creator reports on Reddit and Korean AI communities. Community results are self-reported and not controlled comparisons. Content: Bagaimana jika AI punya 3.992 tools—apakah semakin banyak tools berarti semakin pintar? Belum tentu. Justru terlalu banyak pilihan bisa membuat AI boros token dan sulit menentukan tool yang tepat. Bayangkan sebuah AI agent yang memiliki akses ke ribuan API: search, database, browser, calculator, payment, code execution, dan masih banyak lagi. Masalahnya, jika semua deskripsi tool diberikan ke LLM setiap kali harus mengambil keputusan, context menjadi penuh dan penggunaan token meningkat. ToolNet menawarkan pendekatan berbeda: membuat Tool Graph. Setiap tool direpresentasikan sebagai node, sedangkan kemungkinan perpindahan dari satu tool ke tool berikutnya menjadi edge. Jadi, daripada: LLM → 3.992 tools agen cukup mengikuti jalur yang relevan: Tool A → Tool B → Tool D → Tool E Setelah menggunakan sebuah tool, ToolNet tidak perlu mempertimbangkan seluruh library lagi. Sistem dapat memprioritaskan successor tools yang paling relevan. Yang lebih menarik, bobot transisi dapat diperbarui berdasarkan performa tool: ⚙️ Select Tool ↓ 🚀 Execute ↓ 📊 Evaluate ↓ ⚖️ Update Weight ↓ 🧠 Prefer Better Tool ↓ ➡️ Select Next Tool Jika sebuah tool sering gagal, prioritasnya dapat diturunkan dan backup tool dapat dipilih. Pada eksperimen ToolBench dengan 3.992 API, ToolNet mencapai 0,69 win rate dengan 6.575 token, dibandingkan ReAct yang mencapai 0,61 win rate dengan 8.636 token. Kombinasi ToolNet + Reflexion bahkan mencapai 0,75 win rate. Artinya, AI agent tidak selalu membutuhkan lebih banyak tools. Yang lebih penting adalah kemampuan untuk mengetahui: “Tool mana yang harus digunakan berikutnya?” Ini menjadi semakin penting ketika AI agent berkembang dari chatbot sederhana menjadi sistem yang memiliki akses ke ribuan API dan layanan eksternal. 💬 Menurutmu, AI agent masa depan lebih membutuhkan tools yang lebih banyak atau sistem pemilihan tools yang lebih pintar? Content: "A CI/CD pipeline isn't just about automation. It's about making deployments repeatable and traceable." Working with GitHub Actions on the Spring PetClinic microservices project taught me that a pipeline is much more than a script that runs when you push code. Here's what actually changed how I think about CI/CD, from building and configuring this pipeline hands-on: Every image gets tagged with the Git SHA, not "latest." This sounds like a small detail. It isn't. When a deployed container is tagged with the exact commit that built it, you can trace any running service back to the precise line of code it came from. Debugging a production issue becomes "which commit introduced this" rather than "what version is even running right now." The Git SHA tag is a traceability tool, not just a naming convention. Images push to Amazon ECR, a private registry with IAM access controls. Not Docker Hub. Not a public registry. A private ECR repository means only authorised services and workflows can pull the image. Combined with image scanning, you control exactly what reaches your cluster. OIDC authentication instead of long-lived AWS credentials. This was the security practice that stood out most to me. Without OIDC, you store an AWS access key inside GitHub Secrets, a static credential that exists until someone manually rotates it. With GitHub Actions OIDC and an AWS IAM role, the workflow requests a short-lived token at runtime. No stored credential. Nothing to leak. Nothing to rotate manually. One configuration change that eliminates an entire credential management risk. The shift in thinking that GitHub Actions produced for me: I stopped asking "can I deploy this?" and started asking "can I make this deployment repeatable, secure, and auditable every single time?" Those are different questions, and the second one is the one that matters in production environments. 💬 What's one CI/CD practice you think every junior DevOps engineer should learn early, and why? Content: There is never a single governance problem. It is always many. Most enterprises running Databricks across AWS, Azure, and GCP have built governance workspace by workspace. Each workspace: its own Hive metastore, its own access control logic, its own audit trail that stops at the workspace boundary. Unity Catalog fixes the root cause of all these problems, not the symptoms. One account-level metastore per region. One namespace covering tables, files, ML models, and AI tools. Governance enforced above the table owner, not hoped for at the table level. Modak led a migration for a Fortune 500 enterprise across all three clouds. Results? ● 75% reduction in security administration overhead. ● 30% reduction in platform runtime cost. ● Every asset under one lineage and audit model. The sequencing is what most teams get wrong. Content: 🚀 Delta Lake Optimization Techniques — Complete Cheat Sheet Your Delta tables can become slower over time because of small files, inefficient data layout, excessive rewrites, and poor partitioning. Here are the key optimization techniques every Databricks / Data Engineer should know 👇 🔥 1. OPTIMIZE Compacts small files into larger files → fewer files to scan → faster queries. 📍 2. Z-ORDER Clusters related data based on frequently filtered columns and improves data skipping. 🗂️ 3. Partitioning Use partitioning carefully on columns frequently used for filtering. Avoid high-cardinality partition columns. 🧹 4. VACUUM Removes obsolete data files that are no longer referenced by the Delta transaction log. ⚠️ Understand retention requirements before aggressive cleanup. ⚡ 5. Data Skipping Delta uses file statistics such as min/max values to skip files that cannot match a query. 💧 6. Liquid Clustering Modern Databricks tables can use Liquid Clustering for adaptive data layout without traditional partitioning/Z-ORDER management. 📦 7. Optimal File Sizes Avoid millions of tiny files and avoid creating excessively large files. File sizing should match workload and platform guidance. 🤖 8. Auto Optimization Databricks capabilities can automatically improve file sizing and compaction during ingestion/write workloads. 🔎 9. Predicate Pushdown Filter data as early as possible so Spark reads less data. 🔄 10. Optimize MERGE / UPDATE / DELETE Poorly designed DML can cause unnecessary file rewrites. Optimize the workload and table layout. 📊 11. Change Data Feed (CDF) Capture row-level changes efficiently for downstream incremental processing instead of repeatedly scanning the entire table. 📈 12. Monitor & Maintain Track: • File counts • Table size • Query performance • OPTIMIZE history • VACUUM history • Shuffle & scan metrics. 📌 Save this post for your Databricks interview preparation. 📤 Share it with your Data Engineer friends!
